HISTORY AND ORGANIZATION OF THE UNIVERSITY HISTORICAL SKETCH 

Purdue University was established by the General Assembly of the State of Indiana and is supported by the state with some assistance from the national government. The governing body of the institution is a 

Board of Trustees consisting of nine members, appointed by the Governor, of whom three are selected by the general Alumni Association of the 

University. 

Purdue University is a land-grant institution and owes its origin to an act passed by Congress on July 2, 1862, popularly known as the "Morrill Act." The act offered grants of public land to the several states to aid in the maintenance of colleges whose leading objects should be "without excluding other scientific and classical studies, and including military tactics, to teach such branches of learning as are related to agriculture and the mechanic arts." The act specified that none of the money derived from the sale of these lands should ever be used for erection or repair of buildings. The University received $340,000 from this source, including principal and accrued interest, which sum is held in trust by the state at interest.

On March 6, 1865, the General Assembly of Indiana voted to avail itself of the provisions of the Morrill Act and steps were taken toward the establishment of the new institution of learning. A keen rivalry for its location immediately sprang up and various inducements were held out by ambitious localities. Finally, in 1869, the General Assembly accepted from John Purdue, a philanthropic business man of Lafayette, and other public-spirited citizens of Tippecanoe County, the sum of $200,000 and a tract of one hundred acres of land, and voted to erect the proposed institution in Tippecanoe County, leaving the exact location to be determined upon by the Board of Trustees, pledging the faith of the state that the location so fixed would be permanent. It was also voted, in recognition of the fact that the major part of this splendid contribution came from John Purdue, that the institution should have "the name and style of 'Purdue University'"; and the faith of the state was likewise pledged "that said name and style shall be the permanent designation of said institution, without addition thereto or modification thereof.” 

Purdue University, as a land-grant institution, receives funds provided by the several Congressional Acts known as the Second Morrill Act, the Hatch Act, the Adams Act, the Nelson Act, the Smith-Lever Act, the Smith-Hughes Act, the Purnell Act, and the Capper-Ketcham Act. It thus appears that the University, while bearing the name of John Purdue, is an institution under the exclusive control of the state and supported chiefly by state and federal funds. 

Among the private benefactors are Amos Heavilon, Eliza Fowler, James M. Fowler, William C. Smith, Moses Fell Dunn, Martha F. Davis, William E. Pinney, George Ade, David E. Ross, Mr. and Mrs. Frank M. 

Cary, Richard B. Wetherill, Thomas Duncan, Mrs. W. F. M. Goss, Charles 

H. Viol, Mr. and Mrs. A. E. Viol, Mrs. Charles Major, Henry W. Mar-

PURDUE UNIVERSITY 

shall, Chase Osborn, Mr. and Mrs. George Spitzer, Miss Frances M.

Shealy, Arthur and Alida M. Cunningham, Mrs. Harriet C. Small, George K. Throckmorton, J. K. Lilly, Will R. Wood, Mrs. Charles Bene dict Stuart, Miss Mary Ettie Hamlin, Isaiah Miller, Mrs. Oliver P. Terry, Mrs. Ellen Victoria Ross Kneale, Miss Carolyn E. Shoemaker, Mrs. Mary 

G. Stidham, Mr. and Mrs. Charles J. Lynn, and many others.

The first President of the University was Dr. Richard Owen (18721874), at the time of his appointment a distinguished scientist and a professor in Indiana University. Dr. Owen studied the problem of organization and presented to the Board of Trustees an elaborate and detailed report setting forth his conception of what the proposed institution should be. He retired from office, however, before the beginning of the instructional work of the University. 

Mr. Abraham C. Shortridge (1874-1876), before his appointment superintendent of the Public Schools of Indianapolis, succeeded Dr. Owen in the presidency. During his administration the institution began to function. The instructional work was organized in a modest way in the spring of 1874 under the immediate supervision of Professor John S. 

Hougham, who later served as Acting President of the University. The first regular students were matriculated in September, 1874, and the first degree was granted in June, 1875.

President Shortridge was succeeded in office by Dr. Emerson E. 

White (1876-1883). Dr. White, at the time of his appointment an editor, author, and educator, of national reputation, had been Superintendent of Public Instruction of the State of Ohio. During the administration of 

President White the schools and courses of the University began to assume definite form.

On the conclusion of President White's term of office, Dr. James 

Henry Smart (1883-1900), became the chief executive of the University. 

Dr. Smart had been Superintendent of the Public Schools of Fort Wayne, Indiana, and had served three terms with distinction as Superintendent of Public Instruction of the State. He proved to be a most capable organizer, administrator, and financial manager, and it was in the course of his long administration that the success of the new institution was definitely assured. The intelligent co-operation of Mr. Charles Benedict 

Stuart was an important factor in the success of Dr. Smart's administration. Mr. Stuart, a leading lawyer of Lafayette and a graduate of 

Amherst College, was for many years the President of the Board of Trustees of the University. The united efforts of Mr. Stuart and Dr. 

Smart during these years have been significant in the progress of the institution. 

Upon the death of Dr. Smart in 1900, Dr. Winthrop Ellsworth Stone (1900-1921) was elected to the presidency. Dr. Stone had been for many years head of the Department of Chemistry and Vice-President of the University. During the long administration of President Stone the standards of scholarship were raised, the courses of instruction were expanded and strengthened, the material equipment was enlarged and improved, and the enrollment of the University was very greatly increased.

HISTORY AND ORGANIZATION 

11 Following the tragic death of President Stone in the Canadian Rockies in the summer of 1921, the affairs of the University were conducted for a year by Mr. Henry W. Marshall, a member of the Board of Trustees, as Acting President, and by Dr. Stanley Coulter, Dean of 

Men, Dean of the School of Science, and head of the Department of Biology, as Chairman of the Faculty. At the conclusion of this interim the Board of Trustees called Dr. Edward Charles Elliott, then Chancellor of the University of Montana, to the presidency of the institution. President Elliott entered upon his duties on September 1, 1922. 

The administration of President Elliott (1922-1945) was the longest in the annals of Purdue and in many ways the most distinguished. The dynamic energy of the President was reflected in great material expansion, in enlarged relations off the campus, in the establishment on a firm basis of an extensive system of postgraduate instruction and, with Mr. 

David E. Ross, in the founding and development of the Purdue Research 

Foundation. The concluding phase of the Elliott administration coincided with America's participation in World War Two, wherein President and faculty made notable contributions, personal and scientific, and wherein the multiple services and sacrifices of the alumni reflected honor upon the training they had previously received. Already in the brief period since July 1, 1945, perspective reveals an era of vast accomplishment. 

From July 1, 1945, to December 31, 1945, Dr. Andrey Abraham Potter, Dean of the Schools of Engineering, served as Acting President. 

On January 1, 1946, Dr. Frederick Lawson Hovde succeeded Doctor Elliott as President of the University. 

The University has clung rather closely to the purposes for which it was established. The main purpose of the institution has been to train men for service in the fields of engineering, agriculture, pharmacy, and applied science; at the present time there are more than 28,000 living graduates, and nearly twice that number of former students are engaged in technical and scientific pursuits all over the world. 

While the major part of the work of the University appeals to men, over two thousand women are now enrolled in the several schools of the University, particularly in home economics and general science. 

ORGANIZATION 

The instructional work is organized in the following schools, divisions, and curricula:

PURDUE UNIVERSITY RESEARCH AND EXTENSION 

In addition to the Schools and Departments of Instruction, the University maintains other branches of great importance to the public. 

I. The Agricultural Experiment Station was organized under an 

Act of Congress approved in 1887 "to promote scientific investigation and experiments respecting the principles and applications of agricultural science," supplemented by later Acts of Congress and of the State Legislature. The Experiment Station is a scientific institution with a staff of research workers, separate funds, and laboratories. 

II. The Agricultural Extension Service, formerly called the Depart ment of Agricultural Extension, organized under an Act of the State Legislature of 1911, has for its function the extension of knowledge and the carrying of the results of the work of the Experiment Station and of the School of Agriculture to persons not in attendance at the University. 

Its activities are manifold and various, reaching hundreds of thousands of farmers and others seeking a knowledge of agricultural practice and rural betterment.

III. The Engineering Experiment Station, whose organization was approved by the Board of Trustees on February 28, 1917, conducts researches in the various fields of engineering, cooperates with engineering societies, industries, railroads, utilities, public works, and the Government, and publishes in bulletin form, in papers before engineering groups, and in the engineering press, the results of its investigations. 

Most of the investigations carried on in the Engineering Experiment Station are supported by industries, utilities, and the Government and have included major contributions in the fields of transportation (railway, highway and air transport), heat transfer, electric power transmission, materials, gas technology, electronics, and power engineering. 

IV. A Division of Technical Extension was established by the Board of Trustees, effective July 1, 1945, to coordinate all extension activities of the University except those in agriculture and home economics. Extension instruction, under the direction of the subject-matter departments, is conducted through this division, and includes off-campus classes, both credit and non-credit, correspondence study, short courses, conferences, clinics, lectures, demonstrations, publications, and other formal and informal enterprises conducted on and off the campus. 

The Division of Technical Institutes is administered by the Division of Technical Extension in cooperation with the engineering and other schools of the University. The Technical Institute programs are offered off-campus and furnish specialized, intensive study designed to meet the needs of industry for technically trained persons. These programs are self-contained and lead to Technical Institute Diplomas. Training is offered in six major fields of study: I. Production Planning Technology, II. Drafting and Mechanical Technology, III. Electrical Technology, IV. Industrial Technology, V. Chemical and Metallurgical Technology, VI. Building Construction Technology.

HISTORY AND ORGANIZATION 

13 

Major extension centers at Fort Wayne, Hammond, Indianapolis,

LaPorte, Michigan City, and Muncie administer the Technical Extension program in these areas. 

The Public Safety Institute, also administered under the direction of the Division of Technical Extension, was established in 1936 to serve the people of Indiana in the protection of human life and property. This 

Institute conducts service, training, and research activities to encourage the wider use of organized and scientific methods of accident prevention and public safety.

V. The Purdue Research Foundation was incorporated under the laws of the State of Indiana on December 30, 1930. This act provides a legal device which makes it possible for Purdue University to undertake activities of fundamental importance not clearly within the province of the Trustees of the University as defined by federal and state laws. 

This corporation is organized to promote educational purposes by encouraging, fostering, and conducting scientific investigations and industrial research, by training and developing persons for the conduct of such investigations and research, and by acquiring and disseminating knowledge in relation thereto; and further, both in connection with 

Purdue University and independently thereof, to foster and encourage education and learning in science, agriculture, and mechanic arts and to promote the liberal and practical education of the industrial classes in the several pursuits and professions of life. 

VI. The Division of Educational Reference, approved by the Board of Trustees on May 8, 1925, is directly responsible to the President of the University. It is the function of the Division to study the instructional activities of the University, to serve as educational adviser to both faculty and administrative officers, and to publish the results of its labors in the form of bulletins. The Division also coordinates the research in problems of university administration and instruction conducted by various members of the faculty or by committees of the faculty.

VII. The Statistical Laboratory, approved by the Board of Trustees on July 1, 1948, was established to perform the following functions: to coordinate the teaching of statistics in the University; to organize, sponsor, and supervise research in statistical theory and the application of statistical methods; to provide consultation and advice on statistical methods to research workers; to provide consultation, advice, and statistical services by contract or special arrangements with agencies of business, agriculture, industry, government, and the State; to develop, maintain, and operate a computing laboratory. 

The facilities and services of the Statistical Laboratory are available to students, faculty members, and research workers and by special arrangements to individuals and organizations not directly connected with the University.

GENERAL INFORMATION 

Convocations and Lectures. Convocations include a series of lectures, concerts, and other artistic performances presented at intervals throughout the year. The series is planned by a committee of representative students and members of the faculty and staff. Intended primarily for students, convocations afford students, faculty, and friends of the University an excellent opportunity at nominal cost to hear distinguished lecturers representative of various fields of thought and experience and to enjoy the best in cultural entertainment. 

Religious Convocations. At intervals during the academic year, a convocation for worship is held in the Hall of Music for the students and the staff of the University. These services are non-sectarian, an attempt being made to minister to the spiritual needs of all regardless of faith or creed. A choir of three hundred voices adds beauty and inspiration to the convocations.

Physical Education, Including Athletics. The Division of Physical Education for Men and the Department of Physical Education for Women have supervision over and administer instruction in physical activities, sports, and games, in which all students not physically disqualified are encouraged to participate. So far as possible, physical activity takes the form of recreation in accordance with the taste and adaptability of the individual. In January, 1946, the University established required courses in physical education for freshmen and sophomore male students. In 

December, 1948, because of overcrowded facilities, this requirement was temporarily discontinued. However, a number of elective courses were made available for students wishing to receive instruction in various sports activities. The department of physical education for women offers special elective courses for juniors and seniors. First-aid instruction is available to both men and women students. 

The University is an original member of the Western Intercollegiate Conference, under the rules of which all intercollegiate contests are played. The University is also an original member of the Indiana Intercollegiate Athletic Association (formerly the Indiana Intercollegiate Conference), and for some years has also been affiliated with the National 

Collegiate Athletic Association. Eligibility rules concerning the playing of intercollegiate games are enforced by the Faculty Committee on 

Athletics. 

The Women's Athletic Association promotes a program of recreation for all the women students of the University. 

The Purdue Memorial Union, an organization of alumni, students, former students, faculty members, and friends of the University, in cooperation with the Trustees of the University, has provided a commodious building for the social recreational activities of all students. 

Among its facilities may be mentioned a cafeteria, a dining room, a coffeeshop, a sweet shop, and a residential club unit with 117 rooms for transient guests, a browsing library, a music room, bowling alleys, a 14

GENERAL INFORMATION 

15 billiard room, a game room, two ballrooms and lounges for students and faculty. The offices of the Alumni Association and various student organizations are housed in the building. 

The Student Union Board, consisting of juniors and seniors, assists the administrative management of the Union in developing and supervising student activities centering in the building. 

The Purdue Student Council represents the student body in matters pertaining to student self-government. Its purposes are: to act as an intermediary between the faculty and the students, to control and administer certain matters of primary concern to students, and to make recommendations to the faculty on behalf of the student body. The Executive 

Board is made up of elected representatives from the student body, ex-officio members from student organizations, and representatives from the Alumni Association and the faculty-administration. The Student 

Assembly is composed of representatives from housing units on the campus and recommends action concerning student interests to the 

Executive Board of the Student Council. 

Associated Women Students. All women students of the University are members of the Associated Women Students and are urged to take part in the activities of the organization. These activities include a program of orientation for freshman and transfer women, interviews with new students to encourage participation in a wisely-chosen program of extracurricular activities, conferences on women's work and opportunities, and various social occasions. Associated Women Students is also the governing body for women students. Through its elected officers and representatives, social regulations affecting women students are made and enforced. Moreover, the organization serves as a medium by which social standards of students of the University may be created and maintained.

Publications. The student publications of the University include the 

Purdue Exponent, the daily news of what is going on in all departments of the University; the Purdue Agriculturist, a monthly magazine published by the agricultural students; the Purdue Independent, published bi-weekly by the Purdue Independent Association; the Purdue Engineer, published monthly by students of the engineering schools; the Purdue 

Pharmacist, published monthly by students in the School of Pharmacy; the Purdue Scientist, published by students in the School of Science; the 

Scrivener, a literary magazine published twice a year; the Debris, the annual of the senior class; and the Rivet, a monthly feature magazine of campus life.

Scientific Societies. Connected with the various departments of technical instruction are numerous scientific societies. 

Honorary fraternities are designed to recognize students who have excelled in scholastic attainment and are potential leaders in professional areas. Purdue has professional and honorary fraternities in each of the general academic areas. Most of the organizations are branches of national organizations, and in most of them the undergraduate membership is made up of junior and senior students.

The recognition groups provide honor to students who have shown outstanding leadership qualities in organizations and in contributions to the University.

Specific interest and hobby groups are available to students so that they may gain as well-rounded an education as possible. 

The Inter-Faith Council. The University Inter-Faith Council is de signed to coordinate and unify the activities of the various religious agencies on the campus. Through this organization students have the opportunity of talking with fellow students of numerous church denominations, thus gaining a broader knowledge of other faiths.

The Purdue Musical Organizations consist primarily of the following four groups: the University Choir of 300 mixed voices, the Concert Choir of 28 outstanding voices, the University Orchestra of 60 pieces, the

Varsity Glee Club of 58 men. The organizations and their specialties furnish the majority of entertainment for meetings and conventions on the campus and carry a very full schedule of state and mid-western concerts. Non-credit classes in piano and musical theory are also offered to all students. All the music is extracurricular. Musical Organizations maintains a supervised music lounge with more than 3,000 recordings, and ten practice rooms for interested students. 

The Purdue Military Bands. Students who are good musicians may elect to take the basic course in Military Bands in place of the required course in Military Training and will receive the same credit. The Band is organized as a military organization with student commissioned and non-commissioned officers assuming responsibilities for certain administrative duties. Members may enter the advanced courses in their junior and senior years and receive the same credit as given in the advanced R.O.T.C. The Band plays at athletic events, Commencement exercises, Gala Week, military ceremonies, and many other occasions, and makes several trips with the football team in the fall.

Dramatic Organizations. Purdue Playshop presents a series of plays each year offering students the opportunity to participate as actors or members of the scenery, lighting, costume, and make-up crews. Forensic Activities. Purdue belongs to the Western Conference 

Debating League. Both men and women students participate in intercollegiate debates and discussion programs in competition with students from other universities. Each year several public speaking contests limited to Purdue students are sponsored by the Speech Department, including the Albert J. The Reisner Trophy is awarded annually to students for participation in intramural speech competition. A student speakers' bureau and radio station WBAA present student speakers to off-campus audiences. The

ADMISSION TO THE UNIVERSITY REQUIREMENTS FOR ADMISSION-FRESHMEN 

For admission to the freshman class one must present credits in 15 units of secondary school work. A unit represents the study of any subject for a school year of at least 32 weeks, with five recitation periods a week, each 45 minutes in length, or the equivalent. Two laboratory periods in any science or vocational study are considered as equivalent to one classroom period.

For All Applicants the prescribed fifteen units of credit must be distributed as follows: 

English History or Social Science. 

Schools of Engineering 

3 units 1 unit 1 unit 

All Other Schools 

3 units 1 unit 1 unit 

Elementary Algebra Advanced Algebra 

1½ unit 

Plane Geometry 1 unit 1 unit 

Solid Geometry 1½ unit 

Laboratory Science 

1 unit 1 unit 

Additional English, languages, mathematics, science, or social studies 3 units 3 units 

Other high-school subjects 4 units 5 units 15 units 15 units German is recommended for those who expect to study chemical or metallurgical engineering.

An applicant for admission to engineering who is deficient only in solid geometry but has credit for two units of algebra or a half unit of trigonometry will be admitted but required to make up the solid geometry during his first year. Similarly, one who has credit for only one year of algebra but has credit for solid geometry and one-half unit of trigonometry will be admitted with a deficiency of one-half unit in algebra, which will be considered satisfied when he has passed Mathematics 1. 

It is urged that the applicant for admission to engineering present credit for trigonometery and for a fourth semester of algebra for a total of two units of algebra. It is further urged that the fifteen units submitted for admission include two units of natural science with laboratory work, preferably physics and chemistry. 

It is urged that applicants who intend to earn a degree in pharmacy submit at least two units of science with laboratory work, preferably from biology, chemistry, and physics, in the order named. 

PROCEDURE FOR MAKING APPLICATION 

An application for admission must be made on a form obtainable from the Director of Admissions. It must be filled out jointly by the applicant, by his parent or legal guardian if he is a minor, and by the principal of his high school. No request for admission will be considered 18

ADMISSION 

19 unless the applicant has complied in full with instructions for preparing and submitting the application as given on the official form. The school diploma or any list of credits issued by the school is not acceptable in place of this application.

The University prefers to receive the application at least two months before the beginning of the semester for which admission is requested. 

If the completed application is not received by the Director of Admissions prior to ten days before the date of the applicant's first registration in the University, the applicant may be assessed a late admission fee of $5. 

Applicants who expect to enter direct from high school are advised to apply early, if possible soon after the beginning of the last semester in high school. When the application is received, the Director of Admissions will notify the student of his status as an applicant and will provide a supplementary report form on which grades and credits for the last semester must be reported by the principal. 

The applicant who has attended another college or university must submit the regular application through his high school, and in addition, arrange with the institutions previously attended to forward transcripts to the Director of Admissions at Purdue University. Such transcripts must be submitted even though advanced standing may not be desired. 

Application for a scholarship, for living accommodations, or for any other special consideration by the University does not constitute application for admission, and acceptance in any instance does not imply acceptance for admission. Such negotiations are apart from admission and must be completed with the office responsible for them. 

CUMULATIVE TEST RECORDS 

Cumulative standard test records will be carefully considered in connection with any application. Such records, to be of most value, should (1) cover at least the three most recent years of the candidate's school life, (2) provide information concerning the candidate's intellectual capacity, and (3) include an accurate record of results of comparable (objective) measures of achievement in school subjects. Data obtained from all tests should be interpreted in authenticated comparable terms such as well-established public or independent school percentiles or 

T-scores of the State High School Testing Service for Indiana. 

The Director of Admissions will be glad to examine the application of any high-school student at the end of the junior year (11th grade) and report to him on the basis of his school record and such cumulative test records as may be available concerning the acceptability of his record and program of study.

GRADUATES OF COMMISSIONED HIGH SCHOOLS IN INDIANA 

Purdue University, recognizing that it is an integral part of the public school system of Indiana, will, upon receipt of proper credentials, admit to its freshman class without examination any graduate of a commissioned high school or of a private secondary school in Indiana holding commissioned high-school equivalency, who is able to satisfy in full the detailed requirements as above described.

PURDUE UNIVERSITY GRADUATES OF NONCOMMISSIONED HIGH SCHOOLS OF INDIANA 

A graduate of a noncommissioned high school in Indiana who is able to satisfy in full the detailed requirements as above described will be admitted upon the recommendation of his high-school principal certifying to his ability to do college work and after qualifying on prescribed admission tests. No fee is charged for this examination. Applicants who expect to take this examination should write to the Director of Admissions at least two weeks before the beginning of the semester in which they hope to enter.

GRADUATES OF OTHER SECONDARY SCHOOLS IN THE UNITED STATES 

Graduates of other secondary schools in the United States which are fully accredited by a recognized accrediting agency will be admitted to Purdue University without examination upon presentation of credentials in proper form certifying to the completion in full of the detailed requirements specified above; provided, however, that non-residents of the State of Indiana will be admitted only when they rank in the upper two-thirds of their respective graduating classes in high school. 

The application of a non-resident of Indiana must be accompanied by a remittance to Purdue University of $5 to cover the admission deposit. If the applicant is admitted and registers in the University, this amount is credited on the first semester's fees. If the applicant is admitted and does not register, the amount is not returnable. If the application is denied, the amount is returned. 

ADMISSION WITH DEFICIENCIES 

A high-school graduate unable to satisfy in full the detailed requirements as prescribed may be admitted with the deficiency if his general high-school record is sufficiently good to rank him in the upper third of his class, as certified by the principal of the school. If he should not rank in the upper third of his class, he may qualify for admission with the deficiency by his performance on prescribed admission tests. Any such graduate who does not have credit for at least one unit in algebra and one unit in plane geometry will not be admitted to engineering irrespective of his rank or his performance on admission tests. 

A graduate thus admitted will be required to remove the deficiency by performing additional work as prescribed. He will usually be obliged to omit part of the regular freshman work, and may find it necessary to attend additional sessions in excess of what is required for the regular program of study. Opportunity is given for removal of entrance conditions by examinations. All entrance deficiencies must be made up within one calendar year from the date of admission. 

ADMISSION OF THE SUPERIOR STUDENT WITHOUT HIGH-SCHOOL GRADUATION 

The high-school student who has a superior scholastic record and who has given evidence of well-rounded development during approximately the first three-fourths of his high-school course is given an

ADMISSION 

21 opportunity to qualify for admission to Purdue University without highschool graduation. The regular entrance requirements are supplemented by certain objective measurements of the student's fitness to be advanced in his educational experience to work at the university level. Thereby the University endeavors to recognize and provide for individual rates of learning and achievement.

A non-graduate of high school will be considered for admission, 

1. He has earned credit toward graduation in not fewer than twelve units. 

2. He has a superior high-school record. 

3. He is recommended by his high-school principal. 

4. He qualifies by his performance on prescribed admission tests. 

5. For admission to engineering, he has credit for not less than one unit of algebra and one unit of plane geometry. 

6. He is approved by the University Committee on Selection. 

7. His program of study for the first academic year is approved by the University Committee on Selection. 

Purdue University cannot be held responsible for qualifying students admitted under this plan for high-school graduation, but it cooperates with whatever arrangement the state or local school system may have for awarding a high-school diploma to a successful participant in the above plan.

STUDENTS FROM FOREIGN COUNTRIES 

Applicants from foreign countries will be admitted without examination upon the basis of credentials certifying to the completion of preparatory studies equivalent to the fifteen units as outlined above, and to the full extent and character of their previous education. Credentials in oriental and slavic and certain other European languages must be accompanied by official translations. The applicant must submit satisfactory evidence of his ability to read, write, and speak English. A University 

Adviser for Students from Other Lands assists such students in entering the University and in various other matters after they have entered. 

ADMISSION OF TRANSFER STUDENTS 

The following requirements are established for admission of an applicant transferring from another college or university: 

1. An application for admission on the prescribed form and submitted through the principal of the high school from which the applicant was graduated. 

2. An official transcript of the work done in the institutions previously attended. A separate transcript must be submitted directly from each institution whether or not credit is requested. A personal consultation with the applicant will be required if the credentials are not sufficiently definite. A marked catalogue showing the courses referred to in the transcript should be submitted.

PURDUE UNIVERSITY 3. A formal report from the Dean of Men, Dean of Women, or an authorized personnel officer in the institution last attended. (This report is obtained by the Director of Admissions and not by the applicant.) 

4. For admission to engineering, an average of at least one grade higher than the passing grade for all courses previously taken at a recognized university or college. 

5. Payment of the admission deposit if the applicant is not a resident of Indiana. (This remittance is in addition to the evaluation deposit.) 

6. Receipt by the Director of Admissions of the completed application, including all items specified above, not later than fifteen days before the date of the applicant's first registration in the University. After that date the applicant may be assessed a late admission fee of $5.

If advanced standing is to be allowed, an additional requirement applies: 

7. Payment of a deposit of $5 for the evaluation of the transcript. If the applicant is admitted and registers in the University, this amount will be credited on his first-semester fees. If he is admitted and does not register, the evaluation deposit is not returnable. If he is not admitted, it is returned. 

ADVANCED CREDIT 

Credit for courses in Purdue University will be given on account of work of equivalent character and amount successfully done in another college. On the basis of these credits, advanced standing will be determined. Advanced credit will be regarded as provisional and may be withdrawn by the Director of Admissions upon recommendation of the head of the department concerned or if dependent work is not satisfactorily completed.

When credit earned at another college or university is transferred to Purdue University and is accepted toward advanced standing, the credit is converted into terms of Purdue courses and applied on the program of study. It then will remain for the student to complete the program, and his schedule of courses each term will be adjusted accordingly. It does not follow that the classification in the University or the time necessary for completion of the required work for a degree will be in line with what was expected at the previous institution. 

Credit will not be allowed for a course in which the lowest passing grade was received. Grades are not transferred; only credit in the course is recorded.

For credit in shop work and engineering drawing based on work done in industry or elsewhere than in an educational institution of recognized standing, the applicant must submit letters of qualification from his employers and samples of his drawings and may be required to pass an examination.

ADMISSION 

23 All credentials are submitted with the understanding that they become the property of Purdue University.

University credit for work in secondary schools will be given only on the basis of an examination for advanced standing. 

Credit in individual courses may also be established by examination, for which a fee of $2 is charged for each examination. 

CREDIT FOR TRAINING AND EXPERIENCE IN THE ARMED FORCES 

Training and experience gained by men and women of the armed forces should be made a matter of record for consideration when, upon discharge, they apply for admission or re-entry to the University. Anyone who has withdrawn from the University to enter the services should file with the University his transcripts, course descriptions, and other related material after the completion of any service course of training. 

Such material will be kept on file to aid in the adjustment of the program of study when the student returns to the University. One who expects to enter the University for the first time after his discharge should keep the same material to submit with his application for admission. 

Studies completed through the Armed Forces Institute will be considered as a basis for advanced standing. The University does not recommend the study of laboratory or technical courses by correspondence. 

Correspondence study should be restricted to such subjects as English, mathematics, history, and the like. 

If circumstances warrant when the service person is ready to proceed with a regular program of study, the University may request validation by examination of any credit to be allowed for advanced standing. 

It must be realized that credit allowed on a basis other than the completion of courses of instruction at the University may be applied toward a degree only as it is allowed in a specific course in a prescribed program of study or is accepted by the head of the school for an elective. 

Purdue University is a scientific and technical institution, and its undergraduate programs of study are closely prescribed in terms of requirements for definite professions. The University is in no position to violate or make exceptions to professional standards imposed by law or by professional accrediting institutions. It is not governed by any agreement originating outside the University for blanket credit or for amounts of credit for a particular service training or experience, but each student will receive every consideration possible in helping him to attain his professional objective.

ADMISSION TO THE ENGINEERING SCHOOLS OF GRADUATES OF LIBERAL ARTS COLLEGES 

Properly qualified holders of the degree of Bachelor of Arts or Bachelor of Science from recognized four-year liberal arts colleges should be able to complete the requirements for the degree of Bachelor of 

Science in Civil Engineering, Electrical Engineering, or Mechanical Engi neering at Purdue University in about two years if they submit, in addition to the entrance requirements in force at Purdue University for the

PURDUE UNIVERSITY 

Schools of Engineering, the following college credits, work to be approximately equivalent in content and extent to Purdue University courses: 

Mathematics, 18 semester hours (college algebra, trigonometry, and analytical geometry, 10 hours; calculus, 8 hours); physics, 10 hours; chemistry, 8 hours.

Such college graduates may be registered as junior students in engineering and may be excused from military training, engineering problems, English, and non-technical electives, and from such other subjects as the Dean of the Schools of Engineering may approve. They will find it to their advantage to make up at least in part during the summer session previous to entrance such subjects as drawing, shop laboratory practice, or other required technical subjects of the first two years.

ADMISSION OF SPECIAL STUDENTS 

Mature persons who desire to avail themselves of the instruction offered in any of the departments of the University without undertaking one of the regular plans of study and without becoming candidates for degrees may be admitted as special students. Such students must present satisfactory evidence that they are prepared to take advantageously the work desired.

Application for admission as a special student should be made on a prescribed form to be obtained from the Director of Admissions and should be approved by the dean of the school in which the student expects to register.

TIME OF ENTRANCE 

Purdue University terminated its war-time calendar with the 1946 March Term and returned to a normal calendar of two semesters and a summer session. It will still be possible, however, for a new student to begin his program of study with any regularly scheduled registration, which usually takes place three times a year-in September, January, and June. Consult the University calendar for definite dates. With the exception of a short vacation period in August, the normal calendar will provide for continuous attendance to complete a program of study in the shortest possible time without sacrificing thoroughness of preparation. 

The time required will be governed by the curriculum in which the student is enrolled.

ORIENTATION 

So that the University may obtain specific and definite information concerning the capabilities of new students, and so that they, in turn, may obtain helpful information about the University, all new students are required to assemble at the University a few days in advance of registration for the exercises known as Orientation. Not only freshmen, but all students with advanced standing and special students, are required to participate in Orientation. The sincere desire of the University is to give students who are new to the Purdue campus every opportunity to succeed in their work; and the orientation plan, it believes, is one means of giving this help.

ADMISSION 

25 The orientation activities include physical examinations, meetings with the head of the school to which the student has been admitted, instruction on University organization and procedures, and testing. 

The following orientation tests are usually administered: psychological, English, physical science, mathematics, and a preference inventory. On the basis of these tests and other available information, entering students in certain departments are classified according to their abilities and training. These tests are not entrance examinations, since no student is rejected on account of a low score; the scores on the tests merely afford the University administration an opportunity to place the individual to his own advantage in making assignments to courses. 

The score on the English Placement Tests will determine whether a new student is assigned to English A, 1, or 32. English A is a non-credit course for the improvement of the student's basic knowledge of the English language. English 32 is assigned for the student who demonstrates above-average mastery of English. The student who passes English 32 is excused from English 31. Those who receive a grade 4 or better will also be given credit for English 1.

All students in engineering are required to take an orientation test in mathematics. All students in engineering who are admitted without advanced credit in mathematics are required to take a second orientation test in mathematics. These two orientation tests will serve as a placement test in mathematics for engineering students who do not present advanced credits in mathematics. Students planning to major in mathematics, physics, or chemistry are urged to take both tests. Other students may take both tests.

On the basis of the entrance units and the placement test, students will be divided into three groups and assigned to mathematics courses as follows: (a) The upper group, namely students who make above a certain total score on the two tests, will be assigned to the secondsemester course (analytical geometry). These students will be given credit for the first-semester course. (b) The middle group will be assigned to the regular first-semester course (college algebra and trigonometry) meeting five times a week. (c) The lower group, those students who make below a certain score on the first orientation test, will be assigned to a course meeting six times a week for five hours of credit. This assignment will continue for two semesters, and the instruction will include a rapid review of high-school algebra in addition to topics covered in the regular freshman courses in mathematics. To avoid an overload for students in this last group, one three-hour course or two-hour course must be omitted from the plan of study for each of the first two semesters.

EXPENSES* 

Purdue University is a state institution; therefore the Trustees grant free tuition to all students entering from the State of Indiana. All others are required to pay an annual tuition fee. In accordance with the action of the Board of Trustees on June 8, 1940, the following regulations regarding the resident status of students in Purdue University are now in effect: 

1. No person shall be considered eligible to register in the University as a resident student unless he has established bona fide residence in the State of Indiana, in compliance with these regulations, and has resided in the State at least six consecutive months next preceding the date of his original enrollment as a student. 

2. No person shall be considered to have gained or lost his resident status by reason of his sojourn in Lafayette as a student in the University. 

3. The legal residence of a minor shall follow that of the parents, unless such minor has been emancipated. In case of emancipation the student, in addition to requirements of these regulations respecting residence, shall present satisfactory proof respecting emancipation. Minors under guardianship will be required to present, in addition to the completed application for classification as a resident student, proof of bona fide actual and personal residence in the state at the time of and prior to such guardianship and to furnish such documentary evidence respecting the appointment of a guardian as may be requested in any case. 

4. The residence of a wife shall follow that of the husband. 

5. An alien may register as a resident of Indiana in accordance with the foregoing rules only if he has taken out his first citizenship papers. 

6. The prescribed form of application for classification as to residence status must be executed by each student. Misrepresentation of facts in order to evade the payment of out-of-state tuition shall be considered sufficient cause for suspension or permanent exclusion from the University. 

7. Discretion to adjust individual cases within the spirit of these rules is lodged with the President of the University.

A graduate student assigned to no course, but taking a preliminary or final examination, will pay the registration fee and a special fee of ten dollars.

A candidate for the degree of Doctor of Philosophy, assigned to research courses: 

(a) Who is in residence at the University, pays the full fee of $60 per semester if a resident of Indiana or $160 per semester if a nonresident. UNIVERSITY RESIDENCE FACILITIES 

Purdue University owns and operates a variety of residence facilities for men and women students. These facilities are considered an integral part of the physical assets of the University, and the experience in group living enjoyed by students who reside in them is a valuable part of their total educational experience. 

Residence Facilities for Men. The University-owned and -operated permanent Residence Halls for Men provide comfortable living accommodations for students in attractive, fireproof buildings of brick and stone. At the northwest corner of the main campus adjacent to the 

Fieldhouse and Men's Gymnasium and to other recreational facilities, Franklin Levering Cary Memorial Halls are modern in every respect, with comfortable lounges, reception rooms, and fully-equipped dining rooms and kitchens. Residence in the Halls provides for study and development under conditions from which students may derive the greatest social, educational, and cultural advantages. 

Cary Hall residents have formed a self-governing and social organization known as Cary Club in which membership is automatic with residence in the Halls. The group sponsors house dances, lectures, athletics, musical groups, a photography darkroom, etc.

Faculty sponsors and counselors live in each building. They are selected for their ability to aid residents with their personal and scholastic problems.

In addition to the permanent facilities described above, the Uni versity also has several Federal Public Housing Authority dormitories which are used for the housing of World War II veterans only. Single and double rooms are provided. These buildings are on four sites near the campus, and have been named Seneca Group, Iroquois Group, Mohawk Group, and Chippewa Group. The University also operates a dormitory moved to the campus from a Naval Air Station. It is known as the 

Bunker Hill Housing Facility. This barracks-style dormitory is near the 

Cary Halls in the center of the Seneca Group of FPHA dormitories. On the agricultural campus, the Agricultural Engineering Housing Facility is a convenient barracks-style dormitory for agriculture and forestry students. It consists of certain rooms on the upper floors of the Agricultural Engineering Building which have been designated as sleeping quarters, study rooms, and lounge.

EXPENSES 

31 All the men's residence facilities are now operated at maximum capacity to alleviate as effectively as possible the acute housing shortage. 

The cost of accommodations in the facilities varies, with the type of accommodations, from $110* for rooming facilities only to $550* for both board and single room for the full academic year. For an information bulletin and application form, please write to the Director of the Men's 

Residence Halls. 

Residence Facilities for Women. University-operated residence fa cilities for women students provide comfortable and attractive living accommodations. Three permanent, fireproof residence halls of Tudor design and two temporary units are three short blocks from the campus. 

The permanent Residence Halls for Women are beautiful modern buildings equipped and furnished to meet the discriminating tastes and many needs of university women. Each hall contains generous lounge space, recreation rooms, dining room, kitchen, laundry, and shampoo room, and student living rooms. A soda-fountain grill in Wood Hall central administration unit serves all halls. The temporary units are Navy-barrack buildings which have been adapted to student needs in so far as possible. 

They are freshly decorated throughout, have adequate heating and plumbing facilities, are equipped with attractive furnishings, and have ample study and lounge space.

Women's Residence Hall staff members and counselors, who are especially trained to assist students with their daily problems, live in each of the five units. It is their aim to help the students create an environment in which maximum growth and development can take place. 

Residents become members of the Women's Residence Hall Club automatically. The Club promotes self-government, social events, athletic activities, and a great variety of other social-educational group programs. 

It promotes good scholarship among its members and recognizes achievement in scholastic areas. 

All women's residence facilities are operated at maximum capacity at present to provide accommodations for as many women students as possible. The cost of residence varies with the type of accommodation provided. Board and room is $480-$550 per academic year, depending upon the accommodations provided.*

For an application form and information bulletin, write to the 

Director of Residence Halls for Women, Purdue University. 

By regulation of the Board of Trustees, freshman women, excepting those living in their own homes, are expected to live in the Residence 

Halls for Women, unless excused by the Dean of Women. Application blanks for permission to live outside the Residence Halls may be obtained from the office of the Dean of Women. Women students are permitted to live only in those houses which are registered in the office of the Dean of Women. No woman student should enter into an agreement with a householder without first ascertaining at the office of the Dean of Women that the house is on the approved list. Accommodations for Married Students. The University is operating 

590 three- and four-room apartments on West State Street and the Airport Road. These are in converted 20x100-foot barracks buildings. A stove, ice refrigerator, and automatic water heater are provided, along with certain items of bedroom and kitchen furniture. Rents on the threeroom apartments are $35 per month and on the four-room apartments, $40 per month. These figures include water and electricity, but fuel for cooking and heating is extra. There is a nominal charge for the use of furnishings other than the stove, icebox, and water heater. The prime qualification for admission of a married student and his family to these apartments is that the applicant be a veteran of the Army, Navy, Marine 

Corps, or Coast Guard in World War II. Applicants with children and persons who have a high percentage of disability, regardless of size of family, are given highest priority. Within the above groups, order of placement is based on class standing in the University. Because of the continued critical housing shortage, it is doubtful if any applications can be accepted from new students for the year 1948-49. 

Other Residences for Students. Students not securing accommodations in the residence halls can obtain rooms in private houses in West Lafayette and Lafayette, but are not permitted to live at places not approved by the University. The Director of the Office of Student Affairs and the Dean of Women will assist students in finding living quarters, but cannot, as a rule, find them rooms in advance of their coming. 

There are thirteen cooperative houses, eight for men and five for women. These are large residence houses leased and operated by students. 

All such groups must be approved by the Director of the Office of Student Affairs for men students and the Dean of Women for women students. 

Each house is required to have a house mother who advises and directs in the work of the house. Each student has to contribute about one hour of labor each day and from $25 to $30 a month in money. Admission to these houses is through application to and acceptance by the Cooperative 

Board. 

There are 35 fraternities and 13 sororities. Normally approximately 

2,000 people find living accommodations in these houses. Membership in the fraternities and sororities is, of course, by invitation.

Board, in some cases, can be obtained at the student's rooming place. 

The Purdue Union Cafeteria on the campus has accommodations for serving meals to about three thousand students, and the Home Economics Lunchroom serves noon luncheons during part of the regular academic year. Board can also be obtained in clubs, restaurants, and private families.

Personal expenses of students vary widely, depending largely on the style of living to which the students have been accustomed and the *All rates quoted are subject to change.

EXPENSES 

3333383 amount of money furnished them. Many students, obliged to pay their own expenses, acquire such habits of thrift and economy as to enable them to get through the college year on a comparatively small amount. 

Depending upon the individual's requirements, food costs will range from $1.50 to $2.25 per day if meals are secured outside University facilities. 

Good rooms, furnished, heated, lighted, and cared for, can be had for from $15 to $25 a month for single rooms, and for from $12 to $20 a student for double rooms; laundry work commands the usual prices. Books and drawing instruments may be estimated at $40 to $75 a year. Seventy-five dollars a month is a fair estimate of the necessary expenses of a student, not including traveling expenses, clothing, or University fees. Many students get along on a smaller amount because they are obliged to do so; those who have a much larger allowance are in danger of neglecting their studies and making poor use of their time.

STUDENT SERVICES The Office of Student Affairs and the Office of the Dean of Women are coordinate offices, which serve as the general administrative agencies of the University in all matters pertaining to student life which have not been specifically delegated to other offices. They are the coordinating agencies for the various kinds of personal and group counseling offered students on the campus. Their staff members will assist any student in the solution of whatever personal, financial, social, housing, curricular or extracurricular problems he may present for discussion. They will also be available to parents, guardians, instructors, and others for consultation regarding problems of individual students. Extracurricular programs which will enlarge the student's opportunity for self-development and improve the cultural life of the campus outside the classroom are actively promoted by these offices. Their staff members confer with the officers and representatives of various student groups regarding their group-activity and social-educational programs. An integrated University program designed to meet the intellectual, social, spiritual, and physical needs of students is the primary concern of these offices. 

Part-time Employment. Students who hope to contribute to the payment of their expenses by outside work during the semester should not expect to earn much in this way. The University maintains a Bureau of 

Student Aid for students seeking part-time employment. This Bureau not only accepts applications from potential employees but also receives calls from employers in the University and the local community. Inquiries should be addressed to the Bureau of Student Aid, Executive Building. This bureau is under the joint supervision of the Office of 

Student Affairs and the Office of the Dean of Women. 

Student Health Service. A medical and infirmary service provides a proper medical and physical examination at the time of entrance and opportunity for each student to consult with a competent medical adviser. 

Furthermore, when he must enter a Lafayette hospital or the Purdue Student Infirmary, the hospital charges will be defrayed by the University to an amount of not more than twenty dollars during the regular semesters. A proportionate amount will be defrayed for the summer session. Medicine as dispensed by the University School of Pharmacy is provided upon prescription of the Director of the Health Service. A modern clinical laboratory is maintained. In accidents or emergencies occurring on the campus in connection with University duties, first ai is administered by the Director. For this service each resident under graduate, graduate, and special student paying the registration fee pays the medical and infirmary fee of $5 each semester*, except when specifically exempted by the President of the University.

The facilities of the University Student Health Service are also available to members of the instructional staff with the rank of Assistant *The amount of this fee is subject to change without notice. 34

STUDENT SERVICES 

35 or Instructor who are not registered as students, provided the medical and infirmary fee is paid during the registration days for each semester. 

Medical attendance at the homes of students or at the hospitals and the treatment of injuries received in intercollegiate athletics and of certain specific and chronic diseases are not included in this service. 

An infirmary is maintained twenty-four hours a day for the bed care of students. The cost of this service is $5.50 a day and is deducted from the regular $20 hospital credit. The infirmary can be used for emergency services during the hours when the Student Health Service is closed.

In connection with the medical examination of the members of the freshman class, which takes place at the beginning of each semester, it is desirable to have from the family physician of each freshman any data concerning the medical history of the family, especially such conditions as tuberculosis, diabetes, chronic nephritis, high blood pressure, etc., as well as the past history of the student. Accurate information concerning the communicable diseases proves of great value to this department at times.

In order to prevent epidemics, it is necessary for all entering students to protect themselves, by vaccination or inoculation, against smallpox, typhoid fever, and diphtheria, which cause loss of time from the classroom and often considerable expense. These vaccinations and inoculations should be received before entering the University, so that they will not interfere with the student's school work. The entering student should present accurate information regarding his vaccinations and inoculations at the time of his entering physical examination. If this information is not satisfactory, he then receives necessary immunization. 

A student who has not had a positive or vaccinoid reaction for smallpox during the last five years is requested to have the procedure repeated before the University opens. Students not satisfactorily vaccinated experience difficulty in finding residence while at the University. 

More than three years should not have elapsed since the last typhoid inoculation.

All students showing positive Schick tests for diphtheria should be immunized.

The best eyesight possible is indispensable in obtaining a college education. Please consult your oculist and make any necessary corrections before entering the University.

If there is no family physician, the parent or guardian will fill out the health blank, which is an important part of the student's record. 

Each student should bring his health record to the physical examination. 

Any suggestion that may be made in regard to the supervision of the health of the individual student will be received gladly.

The Speech and Hearing Clinic is operated under the supervision of the Faculty Committee on Speech Defects. All students are examined for deficiencies in speech when they enter the university as freshmen, and a limited number are admitted to the Clinic for remedial treatment upon

PURDUE UNIVERSITY 

written application and the payment of a special fee. Students with hearing deficiencies may receive lip-reading instruction and advice concerning hearing aids.

The Personnel Services of the Engineering Schools include undergraduate counseling and guidance, and both graduate and undergraduate placement. This activity is constantly conducting research in personnel problems and industrial relations. 

The personnel counseling and guidance services start with the freshman year under the direction of the Engineering Administration staff. 

This group cooperates with the heads of the several engineering schools in a similar program available to upperclass students. 

The placement service, in cooperation with the heads and staffs of the Schools of Engineering and the School of Science, aids seniors and alumni of these schools in employment matters. Special attention is given to the placement of alumni and former students returning to civilian life from the armed services and to those who have been forced to seek new positions because of the closing down of war industries. This service also cooperates with the other schools of the University in their employment problems.

The Teacher Placement Office aids graduates seeking teaching positions and advises employers seeking teachers. Credentials prepared for this office are always readily available for use by prospective employers. 

The Teacher Placement Office is also interested in the promotion of teachers in service.

The Placement Service for Women assists senior women and alumnae of the University in obtaining positions in non-teaching fields. Also included in the placement activities of the Service is help given to undergraduate women interested in summer employment. The staff members advise with women students concerning opportunities and requirements for employment in vocational fields.

FINANCIAL AID SCHOLARSHIPS 

Scholarships are granted on the basis of demonstrated scholastic ability. In the case of students who have spent one or more semesters at the University, a grade-point index of 4.5 is required for most scholarships. Persons not yet enrolled in the University may qualify by taking prescribed standardized tests. Inasmuch as the number of available scholarships is limited, the second factor which receives major consideration is financial need. Every applicant is required to submit a detailed personal budget, and his parent or guardian is also requested to submit a statement concerning family finances.

No student may hold more than one scholarship. In general, inquiries concerning scholarships and requests for application forms may be addressed to the Executive Secretary of the Committee on Scholarships, Purdue University, Lafayette, Indiana. Inquiries concerning special scholarships for students in the Schools of Agriculture and Home Economics may be addressed to the Associate Dean of the School of 

Agriculture. 

SCHOLARSHIPS AVAILABLE ONLY TO PROSPECTIVE STUDENTS The 

State. The law of Indiana provides that Purdue University may appoint two students from each county in the State, who, upon entering the University, shall be granted exemption from the payment of certain fees amounting to $35.00 a semester for their first two semesters. appointee must be a legal resident of the county from which the appointment is made. The appointment expires at the end of the second semester; but if the student maintains a grade-point average of 4.5 or better during the first two semesters, renewal is automatically made for the following two semesters, and so on, throughout his University career. If a student's grade-point average for two semesters falls below 

4.5, his State Scholarship is canceled and is not renewed, regardless of what his subsequent record may be. (He may, however, apply for some other scholarship whenever his grade-point index for one semester is 

4.5 or better.)

The State Scholarship may be held during the summer session of the 

University; its value is $17.50 for such a session.

Applications for the State Scholarships should be made through the principal of the high school; the closing date for accepting such applications is announced each year to the high-school principals. 

Special Merit. These are awarded to a limited number of highschool graduates of exceptional ability, personality, and promise. In addition to superior performance on the standardized tests, an applicant must present a superior high-school record and the recommendation of his high-school principal. The holders of Special Merit Scholarships are exempted from certain fees for the first semester and for each of the following seven semesters of residence whenever a scholastic index of 37

888 

PURDUE UNIVERSITY 

4.5 or better has been achieved for the preceding semester. If the student loses the Special Merit Scholarship for one semester by reason of a grade-point average below 4.5, but in a subsequent semester raises his average to the required level, the scholarship is automatically reinstated for the semester following the good grade-point average. 

In the case of Indiana residents, the fee exemption provided by the Special Merit Scholarship amounts to $35.00 per semester; non-residents are exempted from the out-of-state tuition fee of one hundred dollars per semester. Special Merit Scholarships may be used during the summer session of the University, for which the value is half the regular amount-$17.50 in the case of Indiana residents, $50.00 for out-of-state students.

Exceptional Achievement. The University will award two scholarships each year to Indiana students of superior scholastic ability who have demonstrated interest and competence in some field of science (pure or applied) and who are in need of financial assistance. The amount of each scholarship will be determined by the need of the individual student; the minimum amount of each scholarship will be $500 per year and the maximum possible amount $800 per year. The scholarship will be renewed for each of the succeeding academic years of the undergraduate curriculum provided the holder maintains the scholastic and personal standards required by the University Committee on Scholarships. A semester index of 4.75 is required for retention of this scholarship. 

In order to qualify for an Exceptional Achievement Scholarship, a student must have a superior high-school record and must make exceptionally high scores on the scholarship tests prescribed by the University. 

Furthermore, candidates for this scholarship are required to give evidence, through a written report of a scientific project, of their interest and activity in some field of science.

Honorary. The University will award a limited number of Honorary 

Scholarships to applicants who qualify on the basis of scholastic excellence and personal promise, but who do not give evidence of definite financial need. Such applicants must take the same tests that are used in selecting appointees to the other scholarships.

Purdue Alumni Scholarship Foundation. Scholarships awarded by this Foundation are made possible by contributions from Purdue alumni.

39 The amount of the scholarship depends upon the financial need of the applicant and the funds available. The majority of Purdue Alumni 

Scholarships cover either fees or tuition and fees; ordinarily, the University Scholarship Committee will not give serious consideration to a candidate for such a scholarship who is an applicant for admission unless he ranks in the top third of his high-school graduating class, nor to a student already enrolled in the University unless his cumulative scholastic index is at least 4.10. Through the John Morse Memorial Foundation, the Fairbanks-Morse 

Company of Chicago grants three scholarships each year to juniors in the Schools of Mechanical or Electrical Engineering. Application for such scholarships is made through the Executive Secretary of the Committee on Scholarships; preliminary selection of a group of candidates is made by a special committee under the chairmanship of the Dean of Engineering, on the basis of the student's scholastic standing, character, and personality, and his campus activities. Preference is given to students who are in need of financial assistance in order to complete their University education. Final selection of the scholarship appointees is made by the John Morse Memorial Foundation. 

The award is $250 per semester for each of the three students selected. Provided high standards are maintained, similar awards will be made to the students for their senior years. Should one of the students selected attend the summer session, he would receive one-half the regular semester allowance, $125. It is also anticipated that summer employment in the Fairbanks-Morse Company will be available to the scholarship appointees between their junior and senior years, but there is no obligation on the part of the students to accept such employment.

GRANTS-IN-AID State Vocational Rehabilitation. Under Public Law 113 the Federal and State Governments jointly provide rehabilitation services “to render a disabled individual fit to engage in a remunerative occupation." The services include training, guidance, and placement, corrective surgery or therapeutic treatment, hospitalization, and prosthetic devices. Education and training assistance consists of payment of all direct obligations to the University for fees, tuition, etc. Books, class supplies, and subsistence may be provided according to need. A request for service should be addressed to the Supervisor, State Vocational Rehabilitation Division, 

State House, Indianapolis, Indiana.

Veterans Vocational Rehabilitation. Under Public Law 16 the Fed eral Government provides through the Veterans' Administration services to restore the employability which has been lost through a handicap due to a disability incurred in or aggravated by service in the armed forces. 

A discharged veteran with a pensionable disability who wishes to attend Purdue University should address a request for service to the Veterans' 

Administration, Indianapolis, Indiana.

Veterans Readjustment Assistance. Under Public Law 346 (the 

"G. I. Bill") educational assistance for readjustment to civilian life is provided for any veteran who has been in active service for a period in excess of 90 days exclusive of any period of training in specialized training programs. The veteran who wishes to attend Purdue University should address a request for service to the Veterans' Administration, Indianapolis, Indiana. More detailed information concerning provisions for the veteran may be secured by writing the Director of Admissions, Purdue University. 

Financial Aid for the Sons and Daughters of Disabled World War 

Veterans as Established by the Legislature of the State of Indiana in 1941. Any student of the Soldiers' and Sailors' Children's Home or any person who has had his home in Indiana for five years and whose father served in the armed forces of the United States between April 6, 1917, and July 2, 1921, and was wounded, gassed, or disabled, or is suffering from a service-connected disability is eligible for this financial aid. In 

1943 this aid was extended to include children of veterans of the present war.

The exemption at Purdue University amounts to $35 of the total fees of $60 per semester.

LOAN FUNDS 

The University administers a number of loan funds available to worthy and needy students. The first fund was established in 1902, and since that time additional gifts have been received until the funds now amount to $100,000.

Loans are made from these funds upon application to a committee on Student Loans. An application for a loan should be submitted at least two months before the date on which the loan is desired. 

Loans are made in varying amounts, but not to exceed $200 to any one student. Preference is given to juniors and seniors. The interest rate is four percent for the duration of the note and thereafter six percent. The period of the loan is for one year. 

The student should be able to supply the name of an endorser, and the endorser must be approved by the bank with which he does business or by a business firm by whom he is employed or is known. The student should also supply three names to be used as references. Inquiries for loans should be submitted to the Bureau of Student Aid, Executive 

Building.

GRADES AND HONORS 

At the close of each semester or summer session the students in each subject are given grades on their work as follows: 

6-Excellent, to be awarded for unusually high achievement. 5-Good. 

4-Fair. 

3-Passing in minimal objectives only. 

2-Condition, indicating failure to achieve minimal objectives only to such limited extent that credit can be obtained either by special examination or otherwise without repeating the entire course. At the time grade 2 is reported, there must be filed in the Registrar's office a statement of what the student must do to remove the condition. 

1-Failure, requiring a course to be repeated successfully in order to receive credit.

This grade may be given by the instructor at the end of the semester, or by the Director of the Office of Student Affairs or the Dean of Women as a disciplinary grade when a course is dropped because of serious delinquency during the course of the semester. 

As a temporary record of incomplete work, the digit 0 denotes work passing in quality but not in quantity because of unavoidable absence or other cause beyond a student's control. 

The letters S (satisfactory) and U (unsatisfactory) are used in the case of non-credit courses.

SCHOLARSHIP INDEX 

For every student there will be computed, at the end of each semester, a scholarship index by using the following formula: 6No 5N + 4N + 3N3 + 2N₂+ N₁ 

No + N + Na + Na + N + N where S equals scholarship index; Ne, total number of semester hours of Grade 6; Nă, total number of semester hours of Grade 5, etc.;

A cumulative index will be also computed by the same formula, where No is the total number of hours of Grade 6, etc. If more than one grade is recorded for the same course, the course is counted the corresponding number of times in computing the index.
