DEGREES WITH DISTINCTION 

Degrees are awarded at the end of each semester and of the summer session to such candidates as have completed the requirements of their several schools. At each of these periods degrees with distinction are awarded to those completing the undergraduate plans of study under the following rules: 

(a) Distinction at graduation shall be awarded on the basis of all course work taken. Degrees with distinction shall be granted only to those who complete the four- (or five-) year curricula at Purdue, and not to those who complete only the first three years at Purdue. (b) A candidate for distinction must have earned at least seventy hours of credit at Purdue. For any student to qualify for distinction, his scholarship index must be at least 5.00. (c) If the number of graduates in any school who qualify for distinction under rules (a) and (b) exceeds one-tenth of the total number of graduates from that school for that semester or summer session, the number of degrees with distinction shall be limited to one-tenth of the class in that school, and those graduates with highest indices shall be included. (d) of those students who qualify for distinction under these rules, the three-tenths having the highest indices shall be designated as graduating with the highest distinction, irrespective of the schools to which they may belong. (e) No student with a record of faculty discipline shall be included without special approval by the faculty. † No student with a record of faculty discipline is included without special approval by the Faculty.

THE RECOGNITION OF HIGH SCHOLASTIC ATTAINMENT 

A faculty committee is charged with the duty of recognizing students of superior ability and of assisting such students to realize the greatest possible profit from their college careers.

High scholastic attainment is recognized by citation for distinguished scholarship. Those placed on the list of distinguished students, which is published as soon as practicable after the close of each semester, are entitled to special privileges as follows: 

Honor students of all classes are offered the opportunity to do, for credit toward graduation, work in addition to their regular schedule of studies. These additional assignments must have the approval of the head of the school involved. In order to make such additional work practicable the following special concessions may be granted: 

1. Regular assignment of such additional subjects as the schedule will permit. 

2. Assignments outside class under the supervision of an instructor. 

3. Opportunities to gain credit in a subject by special examination. 

4. Special arrangements as approved by the head of the school involved. 

5. Some flexibility in the application of the system of prerequisites to these students.

Detailed reports of special arrangements under Nos. 2 and 4 above are to be filed by the instructor with the dean of the school involved, with a recommendation concerning the amount of credit to be granted.

Students who in the judgment of one or more faculty members merit citation for special distinguished achievement shall have their names 52

PRIZES AND AWARDS 

53 presented through the heads of instructional departments or directly to the Committee on Students of Superior Ability, together with such evidence of achievement as is available. The criteria for selecting students in this group are: (a) original thinking of consistently good quality; (b) achievement other than class work-publication of literary, artistic, or scientific work; (c) work which requires great ingenuity or industry, but which may not lead to definite publication; and (d) independent projects of reasonable magnitude carried out by the student on his own initiative.

Projects carried out by such students may receive special achievement credit. (See page 254.) Students in this group are not eligible for the special privileges listed above for distinguished students.

REQUIREMENTS FOR BACCALAUREATE DEGREES 

Degrees are conferred at the end of each semester and at other times as determined by the faculty. 

A baccalaureate degree from Purdue University involves the satis faction of the following requirements: 

1. (a) The completion, either by resident course work, by examination, or by credit accepted from another institution, of the plan of study in the school in which graduation is sought. (b) Resident study in Purdue University for at least two semesters* and the completion during this period of at least thirty-two semester hours of work in courses regularly open to third- or fourth-year students. 

Students are normally expected to complete the senior year in residence. 

However, with the approval of the dean or head of the school concerned, students who have had at least four semesters of resident study may complete not to exceed 20 semester hours of the senior year in another approved college or university.† For the purpose of this rule, two summer sessions shall be considered as equivalent to one semester. (c) Registration, either in residence or in absentia, as a candidate for the desired degree during the semester immediately preceding its conferment. Upon special request approved by the deans of the schools involved and filed with the Registrar at the beginning of the final semester a student may be registered as a candidate for more than one baccalaureate degree. 

2. The attainment of a grade of B or 4 or higher in at least 90 semester-hours work in all four-year plans of study; at least 70 hours in the first three years of Engineering-Law. 

3. The payment of the diploma fee of five dollars to the Cashier before noon of the Friday next preceding the end of the semester or at such earlier date as may be specified. 

4. Attendance upon the Baccalaureate Address and upon Commencement when such exercises are held. 

* For the degree of Bachelor of Science in Pharmacy six semesters of resident study in a school or college of pharmacy are required. 

Students who have been approved for the combined Science-Medicine or Science-Law options by the Dean of the School of Science may substitute the freshman year of medicine or law in an approved school for part or all of the elective work of the senior year for the Bachelor of Science degree. 

See footnote on next page. 55

PURDUE UNIVERSITY 

A candidate only part of whose work has been done in Purdue University subsequent to September, 1927, must offer only such proportional part of 90 hours of credit with grade B or 4 or higher as is represented by the ratio which the number of hours of credit toward the degree earned by the student in Purdue University subsequent to September, 1927, bears to the total hours required for the degree. 

A student who has failed to meet the requirements of the ninety-hour rule may qualify for graduation by: (a) Repeating a sufficient number of courses in which he has received grades P or 3, C or 2, D or 1, or F and establishing therein grades of 4 or better; (b) Earning grades of 4 or better in additional courses assigned with the approval of the head of the school in which he is registered; (c) Transferring from another approved college or university not more than nine hours of credit, with a grade equivalent to a 4 or better, earned in courses approved in advance by the dean or head of his school, as attested by a written approval filed in the office of the Registrar; (d) Or combining two or more of the above-listed means. 56

GRADUATE STUDY 

Purdue University offers to qualified students the opportunity of pursuing advanced courses and of undertaking research in agriculture, education and applied psychology, engineering, home economics, pharmacy, physical education, and general science. All the technical and scientific departments give courses and direct research leading to the various Master of Science degrees. A smaller number offer major work and research leading to the degree of Doctor of Philosophy. Professional degrees in engineering are offered to those who are qualified by training and experience.

Further information about graduate study will be found in the 

Bulletin of the Graduate School, obtainable from the University Editor.

DESCRIPTION OF COURSES 

The courses listed on the following pages will, for the most part, be offered during the academic year from June 17, 1949, to June 16, 1950. In many cases the session in which a course will be offered is indicated thus: 

Sem. 1, Sem. 2, or SS (summer session). In some cases it is impossible to specify in advance whether or not a course will be offered in any given session. Information on this point may sometimes be obtained from the head of the department.

For each course the first line of the description should be interpreted as follows: first comes the official number of the course; second, its special title; third, the number of hours a week of recitation, laboratory or practice, and outside preparation; and fourth, the class of students for whom the course is required. 1+4+2, cr. 2 

11. Mechanics of Agriculture. 

(el. 1 or 2A) indicates that the course Agricultural Engineering 11 is in Mechanics of Agriculture, is offered for one recitation and four laboratory hours a week, requires two hours preparation a week, gives credit for 2% semester hours, and is elective for first- and second-semester students in agriculture. The abbreviation in parentheses gives the class semester of the students and the initial of the school, the following abbreviations being used:

Aero-Aeronautical Engineering A-Agriculture AgE-Agricultural Engineering AT-Air Transportation Ch-Chemical Engineering C-Civil Engineering E-Electrical Engineering F-Forestry H-Home Economics I-Trade and Industrial Education L-Engineering-Law M-Mechanical Engineering Met-Metallurgical Engineering P-Pharmacy Em-Engineering Mechanics Engr-Engineering PE-Physical Education S-Science 

The prefix "el." or "op." indicates that the course is elective or optional and not required for the students specified. 58

Forestry Camp. 

Must be preceded by Ag.E. 13 or equivalent.

Ten weeks of field instruction and practice during the summer following the sophomore year. The three following courses are required of all those in attendance: Ag.E. 25 (see page 68), For. 34, and For. 50 (below).

Intensive training in forest surveying, silviculture, and mensuration and work in collecting and mounting forest insects. Instruction in the proper use and care of saws and axes.

Forestry camp is held at the Clark State Forest of about 18,000 acres near Henryville, Indiana. Permanent buildings and adequate sanitary facilities are provided.

A special fee is charged for attendance at the camp; students who are residents of Indiana will pay $25 and those who are non-residents of the state will pay $50. In addition, a deposit must be made to cover the cost of subsistence; any unused portion is rebated to the students after the close of the camp.

VETERINARY SCIENCE 

Professor Donham in charge 

Professors Donham and *Hutchings; Associate Professors Bullard, *Doyle, and Moses; Instructor **Washko; Assistants *Delez and *Walkey. 

Courses in veterinary science are offered primarily as service courses for students in agriculture, particularly students whose major study is concerned with animal production and management. This department does not offer courses leading to a degree of Doctor of Veterinary Medicine and thus does not accept students for a major option. The courses offered are designed to improve the student's capacity to deal intelligently with the more common serious diseases of animals, particularly from the standpoint of sanitation, management, and prevention. 

PRIMARILY FOR UNDERGRADUATE STUDENTS 1. Sanitation and Animal Diseases. 

 (el. 7, 8 A)

General discussion and interpretation of the causes, symptoms and results of the common diseases of domestic animals, with especial emphasis upon control and eradication by sanitary procedures. 

Students who have taken other courses in this department or their equivalent are not accepted for this course. 

Professor Bullard. 

* Agricultural Experiment Station. 

**In cooperation with the U.S.D.A.

Director Dodds in charge

This Division provides courses of instruction in education, psychology. and sociology designed to meet the needs of four groups of people. 

Group 1. Students who are preparing to enter the teaching profession or other types of professional service in the schools or industries. Purdue 

University is authorized by the Indiana State Board of Education to prepare applicants for the following types of licenses: vocational agriculture, vocational home economics, vocational trades and industries, regular high school, special high school, high-school principal, and school superintendent. The 

Office of Teacher Licensing should be consulted for detailed information concerning licenses for Indiana and other states.)

Group 2. Undergraduate students in all branches of the University who wish to take courses in education, psychology, and sociology. 

Group 3. Graduate students who are interested in a degree of Doctor of Philosophy which is available in the fields of psychology, agricultural education, and guidance. In psychology, a major may be selected in the industrial, clinical, experimental, child and adolescent, social, or educational area; minors are available in school administration, secondary education, vocational education, speech education, physical education, sociology, and other appropriately related fields.

Graduate students who are interested in a Master's degree. They may specialize in one of the several fields of psychology listed in the preceding paragraph; in agricultural education, home economics education, trade and industrial education; in secondary education, school administration and supervision, guidance and rural education; in sociology and agricultural sociology; in physical education and industrial recreation. 

Group 4. Administrators and teachers in service who are interested in professional growth through courses of instruction and guidance made available by the staff.

Late afternoon and Saturday classes are offered from time to time. 

These are organized to serve teachers and other professional workers. All off-campus courses are administered in cooperation with the Technical Extension Division of the University. 

The Division of Education and Applied Psychology is also responsible for the administration of the curriculum in trade and industrial education leading to the degree of Bachelor of Science in Trade and Industrial Education, and for the administration of the graduate program in physical education and industrial recreation.

For additional information concerning any of the services of the Divi sion of Education and Applied Psychology, consult the Director of the Division.

FIELD SERVICE IN VOCATIONAL EDUCATION 

For information concerning services found below, write to the Director of the Technical Extension Division. 

A. Teacher-Training in Trades and Industry. 

Classes may be maintained in the subjects indicated above by a (†) in any center furnishing a reasonable number of teachers of trades and industry in vocational schools or departments who wish to take the work. A course covers eighteen meetings of the class with the field service instructor for a period of two hours each meeting, when a credit of two semester hours is given, or for a period of three hours each meeting, when a credit of three semester hours is given. A student may enroll in more than one 

Staff in Trade and Industrial Education. 

course. B.

Itinerant Teacher-Training in Vocational Agriculture. 

Purdue University, in cooperation with the Division of Vocational Education of the State Department of Public Instruction, offers field service in vocational education in agriculture to the teachers in the high-school departments of vocational agriculture throughout the state. This work is organized so as to supplement the resident teacher-training as follows: (a) A series of individual meetings or group conferences with the vocational agriculture teachers and school administrators, with additional special meetings and conferences if desired. (b) Contacts with the vocational agriculture teachers maintained by 

Staff in Agricultural Education. 

correspondence. 

C. Itinerant Teacher-Training in Home Economics. 

Resident teacher-training is supplemented by supervision of home economics teachers in vocational departments of high schools, in vocational schools, and in adult classes, through visitation, individual and group conferences, and correspondence.

The Division of Physical Education for Men aims to: 

1. Promote programs of required and elective recreation activities among the students and faculty members. 

2. Provide individual remedial work for students physically unable to participate in normal activities. 

3. Train prospective teachers of physical education, health, and safety. 

4. Train prospective directors of industrial and community recreation. 

5. Carry on a program of intercollegiate athletics. 

6. Provide instruction in personal living for all male freshman students. This course is conducted in cooperation with the Military Depart ment and the Student Health Service.

MILITARY TRAINING Professor of Military Science and Tactics: Colonel John B. Horton, Field Artillery. 

Associate Professors of Military Science and Tactics: Lieutenant Colonels 

J. G. Bowes, and L. B. Cottingham; Majors R. C. Conroy, H. Hunegs, W. O.

Nelson, K. Q. Paddock, T. E. Persinger, and R H. Wise. 

Assistant Professors of Military Science and Tactics: Captains H. E. Attaya, 

Jr., W. E. Bachelor, E. Bennett, H. G. Gordon, J. Overton, P. T. Ryan, and

J. P. Schatz; First Lieutenant J. R. Johnson. 

The Act of Congress under which the University received certain grants of land requires that military training be offered. In order to take advantage of federal aid in the form of money, materiel, and army personnel, the Military Department is conducted as a unit of the Reserve Officers' Training Corps. The course of instruction-four hours a week for the first semester, basic course, five hours a week for the remaining courses-is both practical and theoretical. At the present time it covers the basic military instruction essential for any branch of the Army or Air Force, with additional specialized instruction to qualify the student as an officer in Air Force maintenance engineering and communications, or in the Artillery, Chemical 

Corps, Corps of Engineers, Ordnance, Signal Corps, or Transportation Corps.

The Military Science Department is under the direction of a Regular Army officer, assisted by other officers and non-commissioned officers detailed for that purpose from the Army and Air Force. 

ROTC students selected as officer material will be deferred from induction under the Selective Service Act of 1948, until completion of their academic course, within quotas allotted, provided they agree to complete the ROTC course, accept a reserve commission as Second Lieutenant, and serve on active duty as an officer for a period of two years if called to duty by the President of the United States. 

Military training carries credit toward graduation in the same manner as other subjects. Advanced credit will be allowed only for military training in federally recognized ROTC units. Students desiring advanced credit should request former PMS and T's to forward ROTC records direct to the 

PMS and T, Purdue University, prior to registration.

Military training in the elementary course is required for all physically fit, non-alien male students of the freshman and sophomore classes. Veterans of World War II are excused from military training. Other exemptions are granted only in exceptional cases, and then in accordance with the published regulations of the Department of the Army and the University. 

Uniforms and texts are furnished by the Government. Basic students are required to make a $15 uniform and equipment deposit. 

Military training in the advanced courses is optional. To be eligible, the student must: 

1. Have completed the ROTC Basic Course, or have served at least one year in the Armed Forces and be acceptable to the PMS and T. 

Honorably discharged veterans who have had less than one year but more than six months of service are required to complete at least one year of Basic ROTC to become eligible for Advanced Course Training. 

2. Have two years remaining before graduation or have a total of two years remaining before completing post-graduate work. 

3. Be physically qualified for commission in the Reserve Officers' Corps. 

4. Have not reached his 27th birthday. 

5. Be a citizen of the United States. 

6. Pass a screening test administered by the PMS and T. 

243

UNATTACHED DEPARTMENTS 

7. Not be a commissioned officer in the National Guard, Naval Militia, or Organized Reserve of either the Naval or Military Forces, or a member of the Army, Air Force, Navy, or Marine Corps, or hold a certificate of eligibility for a commission. 

8. Sign a contract requiring him, unless discharged for the convenience of the Government, to complete the course by attendance during two full school years and one summer camp of six or eight weeks' duration and to accept an appointment as a Second Lieutenant, Officers' Reserve Corps, if tendered. Students are not required to agree to accept tours of active duty after graduation, unless deferred from the draft because of ROTC training. 

Formally enrolled members of the Advanced Course: 

1. Receive a monetary allowance in lieu of subsistence (90c per day at present) for 570 days during the two-year course. This ration allowance is in addition to any allowance under the G. I. Bill of 

Rights. 

2. Will be provided with an officer-type uniform, complete with overcoat. 

3. Receive the pay of a Private (now $75 per month) while attending 

Advanced Camp, and travel pay from the school to and from camp at the rate of 5c per mile. (Subsistence is not paid while they are in camp, as food is furnished.) 

4. Use ROTC texts furnished on a loan basis. 

All advanced courses include the following general subjects: military leadership, psychology and personnel management; leadership, drill and exercise of command; military problems of the United States; military law and boards; command and staff; military teaching methods; geographical foundations of national power; military mobilization and demobilization. 

Students who complete the Advanced Course in a satisfactory manner will be eligible to become Reserve Officers in the Army or Air Force. 

Distinguished Military Graduates are eligible for direct commission in the 

Regular Army or Air Force.

MILITARY BANDS Professor Emrick, Director of Military and Symphonic Bands 

The Purdue Band consists of a Brigade Band and two Regimental Bands for military ceremonies, a Varsity Band for athletic events, and a Symphonic or Concert Band for the study and rendition of the works of the masters. Students of the freshman or sophomore classes who are good musicians will be given opportunity to try out for membership in these bands.

Musicians will be assigned to the Band upon recommendation of the Director of Bands and will provide their own uniforms and instruments except those that are issued by the University. 

University credit is given for the successful completion of all courses in Military Bands; the basic courses are taken in place of the required courses in Military Training. 

Members of the Band completing Military Bands 11, 12, 13, and 14, who possess exceptional musical ability, upon the recommendation of the Director of Bands and with the approval of the dean of their school, may take the advanced course in place of a non-technical elective or other required course. Students who complete the four-year course in military bands will receive a special military band diploma from the University. 

All members of the military bands are eligible to try out for positions in the Purdue Symphonic Band, which is composed of students possessing superior ability. During the winter months this organization devotes itself to the study and rendition of the works of the famous composers, including symphonic music.

NAVAL SCIENCE (NAVAL RESERVE OFFICERS' TRAINING CORPS) 

Captain A. C. Wood, USN, Professor of Naval Science; Commander J. W. 

White, USN, Associate PNS; Assistant PNS'S: Lt. Comdr. G. B. Bjornson, USN; Major G. Codrea, USMC; Lt. F. C. Hill, USN; Lt. E. G. Richardson, USN; and Lt. (jg) A. P. Peterson, USNR.

The Naval Science Department, as part of the Naval Reserve Officers' 

Training Corps, was established at Purdue University on November 1, 1945, with its missions: (1) to produce capable Naval and Marine Corps officers, both regular and reserve, who have sound and liberal academic backgrounds with special emphasis on basic principles of the Naval and Marine Corps professions; (2) to build a reserve of trained officers who will be ready to serve their country at a moment's notice in a national emergency. Students are considered to have fulfilled their University obligation for military training by enrollment in the NROTC. 

Applicants for the Contract NROTC must apply for and obtain permission to enter the University in the same manner as any other student. 

Incoming freshman students desiring NROTC as Contract Students must make application to the Professor of Naval Science. Applicants meeting mental and physical requirements are selected before fall registration by the Professor of Naval Science. Their academic program, living arrangements, opportunities for extracurricular activities, and status in the University as selected NROTC Contract Students will be the same as those of all other students with the following exceptions: (1) They will be required to enroll in one three-credit course each semester for a total of eight semesters, for which credit will be granted by the University in the same manner as for courses offered by other departments. (2) Prior to graduation and normally between the junior and senior years, the NROTC Contract Student will make a three-weeks summer training cruise aboard

NAVAL SCIENCE 

249 

a Naval vessel. (3) By the end of the sophomore year, each NROTC 

student must have completed satisfactorily a one-year course in college physics, including laboratory work, and also must have completed a normal sequence of mathematics courses through trigonometry (usually accomplished in high school).

During the freshman and sophomore years the Contract Student will receive no pay or allowances; during the junior and senior years the 

Contract Student will receive commutation of subsistence in the amount of approximately $30 per month. He is furnished uniforms free for his four-year course and all textbooks for the Naval Science courses are furnished without cost to the student. 

Any Contract Student who is eligible for induction under the Selective Service Act of 1948 will, in order to be deferred for his four years of academic work, be required to agree in writing at the time of his enrollment to accept a commission as Ensign, USNR, or 2nd Lt., USMCR, upon completion of his Naval training and obtaining his baccalaureate degree, and to serve, subject to call by the Secretary of the Navy, not less than two years on active duty after receipt of his commission. This does not necessarily mean that the Contract Student upon being commissioned as 

Ensign, U. S. Naval Reserve, or 2nd Lt., U. S. Marine Corps Reserve, will be required (or permitted) to serve the active-duty period unless his services are deemed necessary by the Naval Service. The signed agreement serves primarily to defer the Contract Student from induction in order that he may continue his academic work throughout four years without interruption. 

A large number of the students in the NROTC are "Midshipmen, USNR" and are in a somewhat different status from that of the Contract Student described above. These "Midshipmen, USNR" are selected on the basis of a nationwide competitive aptitude test given in November or December of each year, high-school records, and personal interviews. 

Although they take the same course of training as the Contract Student, they receive additional benefits in that all tuition, expenses, and books are furnished by the Government, and in addition they receive retainer pay of $600.00 a year. Upon graduation they receive commissions as Ensign, USN, or 2nd Lt., USMC, and serve two years on active duty with the option, if selected, of remaining in the Navy as a career. Information concerning this program has been widely disseminated among the various high schools throughout the country. In order to compete for enrolment in the fall of a given year, the applicant must take the examination given the preceding November or December. 

Further details of these two programs, the NROTC Contract and the 

NROTC Regular (Midshipmen, USNR), may be obtained by writing the Professor of Naval Science, NROTC Unit, Purdue University, West Lafayette, Indiana.

PHYSICAL EDUCATION FOR WOMEN 

Professor Hazelton in charge 

Professor Hazelton; Associate Professors Russell and Schwehn; Assistant 

Professor Pease; Instructors Cottrell, Fried, Grothaus, and Sheetz; Graduate

Assistant Leslie. 

The Department of Physical Education for Women (1) administers the physical education requirement for women of two class hours per week during the freshman and sophomore years; (2) provides instruction in personal hygiene required of all freshman women for one semester; (3) supervises the recreation program for all women students in cooperation with the Women's Athletic Association; and (4) offers professional courses on both the undergraduate and graduate level in the theory and practice of health and physical education. 

Seasonal Outline of Program of Activities: 

Outdoor Season (September to December)—archery, bowling, dance, field hockey, golf, swimming, tennis.

Indoor Season (December to April)-Badminton, basketball, body mechanics, bowling, dance, fencing, rifle shooting, swimming, volleyball. 

Outdoor Season (April to June)-archery, softball, bowling, dance, golf, tennis, swimming.

PHYSICAL EDUCATION FOR WOMEN 

251 Medical Examination. All women students are required to have a physical examination given by the University Health Service and the Physical Education Department before assignment to classes. 

Sports Costume. The sports costume must be uniform and should not be purchased before entrance to the University. The cost of the complete outfit is about $6.00.

Locker Deposit. A deposit of $1.00 for use of lock and locker is required of all students registered in practical classes. The deposit is refunded when lock is returned.

Activity Requirement. In order that students may get a varied experience in recreational skills and the maximum personal development from systematic physical exercise, the Department has set up certain goals. 

During the four semesters, a student must be enrolled in a class in (1) an individual sport (tennis, golf, archery, swimming, badminton, fencing, or bowling); (2) a team sport (hockey, softball, volleyball, or basketball); (3) rhythmics (folk, square, or modern dancing); and (4) P. E. W. 52, the body mechanics course, given usually during the indoor season. Swimming should be taken in the freshman year unless the Purdue Swimming Test is passed.

The individual and team sport requirement can be met by participation in the W.A.A. intramural program outside class hours provided the student meets the requirements of that sport as set up by the W.A.A. and is recommended by the instructor in charge. 

Professional Training. Students desiring an Indiana state teacher's license in physical education should follow the teaching options outlined in the plans of study of the Schools of Science and of Home Economics. Women students whose major interest is in teaching physical education should register in the School of Science. For the state requirements in professional subjects, see the Division of Education and Applied Psychology, page 218, and for requirements for the M.S. degree in Education or Psychology, consult the bulletin of the Graduate School.

PLANS OF STUDY 

On the following pages are outlined the plans of study leading to the 

Bachelor's degree in the several schools.

The semester hour is the unit of University credit. It represents a total of three hours of work per week throughout the semester by the average student. In the plans of study that follow, the number of semester-hours credit for each course is indicated by the figures in parentheses preceding the course titles.

For descriptions of the courses see pages 60 to 253, with index on page 59. 

INDIVIDUAL ACHIEVEMENT CREDITS 

The Executive Committee of the Faculty may award to any undergraduate student credits for work accomplished independently and apart from curriculum and classroom requirements, it being shown that such work represents creative abilities, and affords evidence of personal development, professional attainment, and power for social usefulness. Such "achievement" credits may be substituted for elective courses of instruction as determined in each case by the Executive Committee, upon the recommendation of the Dean of the School concerned. 

BACCALAUREATE THESIS 

In certain plans of study the assignment of a thesis in lieu of three or six hours of elective course work may be permitted, if such assignment is approved by the head of the school in which the student is registered. In such case the thesis assignment shall be included in the student's schedule, and the special thesis assignment blank with the title shall be filed with the Registrar at least three months before the expected date of graduation. The finished thesis in prescribed form must be deposited with the Registrar before noon of the Friday preceding the end of the semester or summer session or at such earlier date as may be specified. 254

AGRICULTURE 

Undergraduate Instruction. The School of Agriculture offers a number of eight-semester plans of study leading to the degree of Bachelor of Science in Agriculture, and also offers two plans of study leading to the degree of Bachelor of Science in Forestry. The schools of engineering and the School of Agriculture offer a four-year plan of study leading to the degree of Bachelor of Science in Agricultural Engineering. All these programs of study provide an opportunity for a broad scientific education with the proper amount of specialization in certain fields of training. 

A plan is provided whereby those who do not wish to spend more than two years in the University may be admitted as special students in agriculture. The special-student programs of study are prepared in consultation with the Dean of the School of Agriculture. 

A large number of courses of instruction in technical agriculture are given by the Departments of Agricultural Botany, Agricultural 

Chemistry, Agricultural Economics, Agricultural Engineering, Agronomy, Animal Husbandry, Dairy Husbandry, Entomology, Forestry, Horti culture, Poultry, and Veterinary Science. Agricultural students receive instruction in the sciences of botany, zoology, chemistry, and physics, which are fundamental to agricultural work, and in English, history, literature, education, economics, and mathematics. 

Certain courses are required of all students in each of the eight semesters; others are elective and may be chosen upon approval of the 

Dean and the head of the department. Freshmen are required to attend weekly agricultural assemblies. Students may be required to take inspection trips in connection with certain plans of study. 

By proper choice of electives students may fit themselves for practical work as farm operators or managers, or for scientific work in the above-mentioned fields.

While the agricultural courses are designed to train students for the farm and life in the country, they aim at the same time to fit men for a variety of very excellent positions in educational, scientific, and commercial work in connection with institutions and industries closely allied with agriculture. The major in Agricultural Administration under the 

Agricultural Economics Option is specifically designed to train students for managerial positions in agricultural businesses and allied activities. 

Graduate Instruction. Graduate work leading to the Master's degree is offered in most of the departments of the School of Agriculture. For information concerning this type of training, refer to the Bulletin of the Graduate School. Graduate work for the degree of Doctor of 

Philosophy is offered in a number of departments. Candidates for this degree may elect courses from approved subject-matter options in the various fields, while the research is done in the laboratories of one or more departments in accordance with the program developed by the student in cooperation with his advisory committee. The program chosen must have the approval of the Dean of the Graduate School. 

A bulletin of Purdue University, entitled The Graduate School, is available and may be obtained upon request.

AGRICULTURAL CHEMISTRY

AGRICULTURAL CHEMISTRY 

(Total credits—freshman, sophomore, junior, and senior years— 

148 semester hours.)

The agricultural chemistry option prepares students for chemical service in industries and institutions concerned with the products of agriculture. These include the food, feed, fertilizer, and pharmaceutical industries, state experiment stations, and U. S. Department of Agriculture and other agricultural research and control laboratories. The curriculum provides an excellent background for graduate work in biochemistry and other plant and animal sciences.

AGRICULTURAL ECONOMICS AGRICULTURAL ECONOMICS 

146 semester hours- 

Agricultural Administration-146 semester hours)

Agricultural Economics offers training which will be helpful for students who contemplate employment as farm operators, farm managers, extension workers, government employees, and employees in farm finance, in marketing, and in managerial or submanagerial positions in agricultural businesses. It also prepares qualified students to take graduate work as further preparation for college or government work or for commercial economic research work. 

Not less than a total of 30 semester hours of agricultural economics and economics must be taken during the junior and senior years. 

Because of the increasing opportunity for agricultural graduates to enter managerial or submanagerial positions with agricultural businesses or businesses allied to agriculture, a special curriculum is offered in Agricultural Administration open to juniors and seniors approved by the head of the Department of Agricultural Economics.

AGRICULTURAL ENGINEERING AGRICULTURAL ENGINEERING 

160% semester hours)

The Schools of Engineering and the School of Agriculture offer an eight-semester-plus-summer-session plan of study leading to the degree of Bachelor of Science in Agricultural Engineering. Students wishing to take this curriculum should enter as freshmen in the Schools of Engineering and follow the curriculum outlined in full on pages 287 and 296. 

This curriculum prepares the student for engineering service in rural communities; for teaching, research, and extension work with colleges, experiment stations and governmental agencies in the fields which require engineering application; for positions in the manufacture and sale of farm machinery and farm-power equipment; for advisory and managerial posts in connection with agricultural development; for positions with farm buildings and materials concerns; and in the increasing use of electricity in agriculture.

DAIRY HUSBANDRY DAIRY HUSBANDRY 

Dairy Production, 146 semester hours; Dairy Manufactures, 148% semester hours)

The dairy production option is suggested for students who wish to specialize in dairy farming and prepare for positions as managers of dairy farms, or as dairy field men, and for students who wish to prepare themselves for teaching or extension work in the feeding, breeding, and management of dairy cattle.

The dairy manufactures option is suggested for students who wish to specialize in and prepare for positions requiring training in the manufacture of butter, ice cream, cheese, market milk, and condensed milk.

This option prepares the students for positions in teaching and extension, and for numerous government and commercial positions which require dairy manufactures training.

ENTOMOLOGY ENTOMOLOGY 

147% semester hours; Pest Control, 145 semester hours)

The entomology option provides a thorough college education and a training for students who wish to prepare for any one of many entomological vocations: as entomologists in federal and state experiment stations and extension departments; for sales promotion or research with insecticide industries; as consultant and service entomologists; in the field of regulatory entomology; as museum curators and city, county, state, or industrial entomologists; and for advanced or graduate study as a further preparation for research and college teaching. The work of the general economic entomologist necessitates certain fundamental training in agriculture and allied sciences such as is required in the regular freshman and sophomore years.

Because of the increasing importance of commercial pest control, the Entomology Department now offers a four-year curriculum that provides for specialization in the technique and practice of industrial and structural pest control. Major specialization begins in the junior year.

FORESTRY FORESTRY 

The Department of Forestry offers two eight-semester undergraduate plans of study leading to the degree of Bachelor of Science in Forestry. 

Instruction given in forestry by the Department of Forestry is recognized and approved by accrediting agencies as meeting the highest professional standards.

The aim of the forestry curricula at Purdue University is to give the student a broad training in the fundamental concepts of his chosen field. To accomplish this aim the student is given a thorough background in the physical and biological sciences. Upon this science background is built the professional instruction in the field of his choice. 

Professional instruction in the Forest Production curriculum is designed to train the student in the management of non-agricultural lands. First emphasis is placed upon timber production, but the closely allied fields of game management, forest recreation, and soil and water conservation are also included. Graduates of this curriculum are adequately trained to undertake the management of non-agricultural lands in the central hardwood region. 

Instruction in the Wood Technology and Utilization curriculum is designed to train the student in the conversion, manufacture, and use of wood. Special emphasis is placed upon the technical properties of wood, both as they affect its use in its original form, and as a raw material for further remanufacture. With the background provided by their technical training, supplemented by some industrial experience, graduates of this curriculum are qualified for positions in several of the many phases of the wood utilization industry.

It is recommended that students interested in any specific field of forestry should plan on a year or more of graduate study.

SHORT COURSES 

285 

SHORT COURSES AND CONFERENCES EIGHT-WEEKS COURSES IN AGRICULTURE 

These courses are designed to meet the needs of those who from lack of money, time, or preparation may be unable to take the regular eight-semester plan of study. The work consists of lectures, laboratory exercises, and demonstrations arranged primarily to meet the needs of prospective farmers. The chief object of the work is to make better farmers to help young men and women to produce better fruit, flowers, and vegetables, better livestock and poultry, and to obtain greater satisfaction and profit from the time, energy, and money expended. 

These plans of study require eight weeks, and one may profitably spend two or three or four terms in the work without duplication. A suitable certificate is granted to those who satisfactorily complete any one of these plans of study. 

The plan of study in dairy manufactures is arranged to prepare and fit students for commercial positions in dairy manufacturing plants. 

Many excellent positions are open to well-trained butter makers, ice cream makers, cheese makers, and others who are thoroughly trained in the manufacture of dairy products. 

A special circular giving full information on eight-weeks courses may be obtained on application to the University Editor. 

Five plans of study are offered: 

1. A General Course in Agriculture. 

2. An Animal Husbandry Course. 

3. A Dairy Production Course. 

4. A Dairy Manufactures Course. 

5. A Country Elevator Business Course. 

ANNUAL AGRICULTURAL CONFERENCE-FARMERS' WEEK 

Farmers' Week is full of good things for busy farmers. The instruction is practical and given at a time—one week in January each yearwhen farmers can take advantage of it. A definite program is outlined. 

Conferences, lectures, laboratory practice and demonstrations in soils and crops, livestock, dairying, horticulture, agricultural engineering, botany, entomology, poultry, and home economics are given. The state agriculture and livestock associations hold their meetings at the University during this week. The State Corn Show is held in connection with the 

Farmers' Week. 

SPECIAL SHORT COURSES 

Special short courses of from five to ten days in length are offered from time to time by the different departments in the School of Agriculture. These cover the subjects of dairying, grain grading, horticulture, farm business, poultry, tractors, veterinary science, etc. Information may be obtained from the Dean of the School of Agriculture.

ENGINEERING Undergraduate instruction in the Schools of Aeronautics, Agricul tural Engineering, Chemical and Metallurgical Engineering, Civil Engineering and Engineering Mechanics, Electrical Engineering, and Mechanical Engineering, leads to the degree of Bachelor of Science.

A special curriculum in engineering-law gives an engineering foundation for the study of law. 

Well-prepared students can usually complete the plan of study leading to the degree of Bachelor of Science in any of the engineering curricula in four years. Many students, however, may find it advantageous to devote more than four years to the undergraduate engineering programs of study by pursuing at one time, in any semester, fewer studies than are regularly prescribed. In cases of inadequate secondary preparation, poor health, or financial necessity requiring much time for outside work, the undergraduate course should be extended to five years or longer. A student who so desires may devote five years to his undergraduate work and include additional instruction in the humanities, the social sciences, the physical sciences, or mathematics. 

A student enrolled in engineering must have earned a cumulative scholarship index of at least 3.2 (see page 50) at the end of his second semester, in order to continue in engineering. Similarly, at the end of his fourth semester he must have a cumulative index of 3.2 to continue in any of the engineering schools.

Advanced courses and research problems leading to the degrees of Master of Science or Doctor of Philosophy may be elected in the various special fields of engineering by those who have completed a standard four-year engineering college curriculum. Details concerning graduate study in engineering will be found in a special bulletin on graduate study. 

Business Training for Engineering Students. Students of Purdue 

University in the major engineering curricula who intend, upon graduation from Purdue, to supplement their engineering preparation with basic instruction in business by becoming candidates for a Master's degree in Business Administration at Indiana University, should include in their undergraduate curricula the following subjects: economics, 6 hours; accounting, 3 hours (6 hours recommended); industrial management, 3 hours; also some background in courses such as statistics, money and banking, corporation finance, marketing, and business law. Students may ordinarily expect to devote two semesters plus one summer session (minimum) to four semesters (maximum) to complete the requirements for a Master's degree in Business Administration at Indiana University, depending upon the number of pre-business courses completed at the time of the transfer. Students must have an index of 4.5 or better earned at 

Purdue University to be admitted to the School of Business at Indiana 

University under the above plan. 286

FRESHMAN ENGINEERING 

287 

FRESHMAN ENGINEERING 

In order to give the student sufficient time to adjust himself and to choose the branch of engineering for which he is best adapted, the program of study during the freshman year is common for the curricula in aeronautical engineering, air transportation, agricultural engineering, chemical engineering, civil engineering, electrical engineering, mechanical engineering, metallurgical engineering, and engineering-law. Lectures and conferences will guide the student so that by the end of the second semester he may be in a position to make proper selection.

CHEMICAL ENGINEERING CHEMICAL ENGINEERING 

(Total credits-160 semester hours)

The plan of study in this school is designed for those who wish to prepare themselves for technical, commercial, sales, or executive positions, not only in the important group of industries known specifically as chemical, but also in a wider group based on the application of chemical principles to manufacturing processes in general. The preparation of the chemical engineer must accordingly include both chemistry and engineering. 

Students who have completed high-school chemistry or received a high grade in the orientation tests are urged to elect Chem. 21 and 22 in the freshman year.

For a freshman engineering student to be promoted to the sophomore class in the School of Chemical and Metallurgical Engineering, he must satisfy the following requirements: (1) If he has been assigned to Chem. 21-22, his grade must be 3 or better in each of these courses. (2) If he has been assigned to Chem. 1-2, his grade must be 4 or better in each of these courses. (3) For students who fail to meet the requirements but still want to enter Chemical or Metallurgical Engineering, a qualifying re-examination will be held.

When practicable, inspection trips to representative industrial plants are made during the last four semesters. (2 or 3)

METALLURGICAL ENGINEERING METALLURGICAL ENGINEERING 

(Total credits-160% semester hours)

This curriculum has been planned for those who wish to prepare themselves for technical, commercial, sales, or executive positions not only in the concentration of ore, reduction and refining of metals, but also in the general industrial field where metals are pressed, cast, welded, electroplated, forged, extruded, or otherwise physically changed to meet the demands of industry. The preparation of the metallurgical engineer must accordingly include both chemistry and engineering. Students who have completed high-school chemistry or received a high grade in the orientation tests are urged to elect Chem. 21 and 22 in the freshman year. 

The demands of industry for new alloys with new combinations of properties as well as for more efficient methods of recovery in the face of our diminishing supplies of high-grade ores make this field an increasingly important one. The mechanical, electrical, civil, and chemical engineers alike are meeting new conditions of service and design which demand new materials.

When practicable, inspection trips to representative industrial plantare made during the last four semesters.

CIVIL ENGINEERING CIVIL ENGINEERING AND ENGINEERING MECHANICS The School of Civil Engineering and Engineering Mechanics offers plans of study leading to degrees in Civil Engineering or in Engineering 

Mechanics. Civil Engineering offers three options, General, Construction, and Sanitary Engineering. 

Civil Engineering is composed of the following divisions: Construc tion, Highway, Hydraulic, Railway, Sanitary, and Structural Engineering;

Surveying, City Planning, and Soil Mechanics. 

The combined School includes instructional laboratories in Materials 

Testing, Experimental Stress Analysis, Soil Mechanics and Hydraulics, and a permanent Summer Surveying Camp. Highway Research Labora tories, including a cold room, are maintained for highway research as a cooperative project between the State Highway Commission and the 

Engineering Experiment Station of Purdue. 

The first four semesters of these curricula deal primarily with fundamental engineering sciences. The last four are devoted largely to a study of the principles of practice and to an intensive training in the analysis and design of engineering structures. 

The curricula offer opportunities for the students to elect courses of a non-technical character.

In the spring of each year a Road School, attended by street and highway officials, contractors, materials and equipment men, and others, from the entire state, is conducted by the Highway Engineering Staff, in cooperation with the Technical Extension Division.

ELECTRICAL ENGINEERING 

(Total credits-153% semester hours)

The plan of study in Electrical Engineering provides fundamental training for the various branches of the profession. Engineering instruction is given throughout all eight semesters of the curriculum; thus a student may determine early in his career whether he is interested in and has aptitudes for this profession. Non-technical courses also are provided in all eight semesters in order that the graduate may be as broadly trained as possible. Specialization is made possible through elective lines of technical study in the senior year. (3)

ENGINEERING-LAW 

315 At the end of the sixth semester the student will transfer to the Indiana University School of Law and enter upon the regular professional curriculum there. Upon the successful completion of the three-year curriculum leading to the degree of LL.B.* at Indiana University, he will be entitled to the degree of Bachelor of Science in Engineering-Law from Purdue University. A student is expected to have a cumulative index of 4 or better on work done at Purdue University to be recommended for admission to the Indiana School of Law. 

A student may enter upon the professional work of the School of Law with an engineering degree and become a candidate for the degree J.D. The requirements for this degree are set out in the bulletin of Indiana University.

HOME ECONOMICS 

The plan of study in Home Economics has two functions: to give the student training which will fit her to become a responsible citizen and an intelligent homemaker and housekeeper; to train her for a skilled occupation by which she may become self-supporting. 

The graduate from this school should be able to plan, equip, and manage a home successfully; to feed and clothe her family adequately; to use the best methods of caring for children; and to understand her responsibilities as a citizen toward the community, the town, and the state in which her home is situated. 

Young women trained in home economics have the opportunity to become any of the following: teachers and supervisors in the elementary and secondary schools and colleges, extension specialists, dietitians in hospitals and other institutions, managers of lunchrooms and tearooms, costume designers, demonstrators for commercial manufacturing concerns, writers for magazines and newspapers, nutrition workers, girls' club leaders, interior decorators, and home demonstrators in extension. 

All students except those in Group F carry the same course through the freshman year; but during the sophomore, junior, and senior years the student has the opportunity to specialize through optional groups of electives.

PHARMACY 

(Total credits-143% semester hours)

The School of Pharmacy offers an eight-semester plan of study presenting opportunities to those who wish to train themselves thoroughly for the important public health and business duties of the retail, professional, hospital, or manufacturing pharmacist, or the pharmaceutical chemist. In particular this plan of study prepares students for private practice and for responsible laboratory positions with the state or federal government or with hospitals, manufacturing establishments, wholesale houses, and importers. Pure food and drug legislation has created many such positions. The best laboratory positions are for men whose education has been broad and general, supplemented with the necessary professional training in pharmacy.

In the past the School of Pharmacy has admitted students directly from high school. Now students take a year of pre-pharmacy courses followed by a three-year professional program in the School of Pharmacy. 

Effective January 1, 1949, students who expect to apply for admission to the School of Pharmacy with sophomore standing should enroll as freshmen in the School of Science (Pre-pharmacy Option). 

Students taking the pre-pharmacy year in colleges other than the School of Science, Purdue University, should submit 30 or more semester hours of credit including the following:

General Inorganic Chemistry Mathematics (algebra and trigonometry) English Composition Speech or Rhetoric Botany Zoology Approved Electives

If an applicant has the required number of hours of academic credit but does not have credit for all prescribed subjects, he may be admitted with 8 semester hours of deficiency, which must be made up before graduation. 

329

PHARMACY 

Students who have completed the pre-pharmacy year at Purdue or elsewhere cannot be assured of admission to the School of Pharmacy. 

When the number of qualified applicants exceeds the available facilities, preference will be given to residents of Indiana, and selection of students will be made on the basis of qualifications. A committee on selection will take into consideration evidence of the applicant's character, intelligence, fitness to study pharmacy, and letters of recommendation, in addition to his scholastic standing. In practice, applicants are first screened on a basis of intellectual qualifications as ascertained from their previous academic records. In the group judged capable of meeting the academic requirements of the pharmacy curriculum, selection will then be made on the basis of character and personality as determined by the results of personal interview, letters of recommendation, and professional aptitude, as well as other tests. 

Students will enter the professional program of study in the School of Pharmacy only at the beginning of the fall semester of each academic year.

Three years' residence in an accredited school or college of pharmacy is required to qualify for the degree of Bachelor of Science in Pharmacy.

Advanced study and research leading to the degree of Master of Science or Doctor of Philosophy, with majors in pharmacy, industrial pharmacy, hospital pharmacy, pharmaceutical chemistry, pharmacology, and pharmacognosy, may be elected in the School of Pharmacy by those who have completed an acceptable four-year college curriculum. Details concerning the requirements and programs of graduate study in pharmacy will be found in the bulletin of the Graduate School. 

The requirements of the laws of Indiana regulating the professional training and licensing of pharmacists are more than satisfied by the training furnished in this school.

The School of Pharmacy holds membership in the American Association of Colleges of Pharmacy and is fully accredited by the American 

Council on Pharmaceutical Education.

SCIENCE 

The School of Science provides both introductory and advanced courses in the various fields of science as well as other subjects essential to a broad education, such as economics, English, government, history, modern languages, and speech. Certain courses are required of all students; the remainder are elective and may be chosen with the advice and approval of the student advisers so as to insure a well-balanced program. In the School of Science, the student may prepare for a vocation in one of the scientific fields or for admission to a medical, dental, or law school*, or may obtain a general scientific education. 

Those wishing to qualify for an Indiana teacher's license should make this known to their advisers as early as possible so that their programs may be properly planned.†

Effective January 1, 1949, the School of Pharmacy of Purdue Uni versity will no longer admit high-school graduates. Students expecting to study pharmacy should register in the School of Science for the Pre-pharmacy Option. They will then apply for transfer to the School of Pharmacy at the end of the freshman year. This application should be filed before April 1.

Students of exceptional ability who desire a broad scientific education but do not wish to specialize, may be admitted to the Liberal Science 

Curriculum, after conference with its Director.

Required Courses. The plan of study of all students in the School of Science must include the following required courses: two semesters of economics, four semesters of English and speech, four semesters of one modern language, two semesters of government, two semesters of history, two semesters of mathematics, two semesters of any three of the following sciences-biology, chemistry, physics, geology, and an additional two semesters with laboratory work in one of the three sciences previously taken or in laboratory psychology, or two semesters in mathematics. 

A total of 147 semester hours is required for graduation under any option except the Liberal Science Curriculum. 

By cooperative arrangement, the senior year may be replaced by the first year in the law or medical schools of Indiana University provided all required courses have been completed and the grades are sufficiently high to satisfy the 90-hour rule.

These students must include in their programs Psy. 1 and 2, Educ. 3, 4, 17, and 18 in addition to requirements in the subjects they wish to teach. 333

In order to give the student sufficient time to adjust himself and to choose intelligently the option for which he is most adapted, three programs of study for the first year cover all options. There is one program for those planning to major in chemistry, mathematics, or physics, another for pre-pharmacy and those planning to major in one of the biological sciences, and a third program for all other options.

THE LIBERAL SCIENCE CURRICULUM 

This curriculum is designed for students of exceptional ability who desire a broad cultural education with an emphasis upon the contributions of the sciences to the modern world plus specialized training leading toward a vocation. One of the special features of the curriculum is the natural science courses which, along with sound training in the subject matter and laboratory technics found in the typical natural science courses, stress the social implications of developments in the fields of science and the relationship between the natural sciences and other fields of culture. Options in English, history, economics, government, mathematics, modern languages, education, physical education, sociology, psychology, and the natural sciences may be arranged by consultation with the Director of the Liberal Science Curriculum and approved by the Dean of the School of Science. Options will not be limited to courses in the 

School of Science. Each student will be expected to have made a decision by the end of the sophomore year as to the vocation for which he plans to prepare. His program for the junior and senior years will be focused upon preparation for that vocation. During this period the student is expected to concentrate his courses in closely allied fields. Arrangements for additional work with appropriate additional credit may be made with instructors in the various courses chosen. 

Students in the Liberal Science Curriculum are enrolled in the School of Science. They will earn the degree of Bachelor of Science upon completion of the curriculum requirements, 147 hours for persons who entered before 1944, or 137 hours for those who entered in 1944 or thereafter.

Total credits-Option A, 145% semester hours;

An eight-semester plan of study is offered consisting of required and elective courses leading to the degree of Bachelor of Physical Education.

The first four semesters are common, except for electives, for all students. 

During the last four, students may specialize in either of two specific fields: (A) physical education and athletic coaching, (B) school, community, and industrial recreation. 

Option A. The physical education and athletic coaching program includes courses totaling (a) 21 semester hours in psychology and education; (b) 49% semester hours in physical education; (c) 48 semester hours in the regular sciences and allied subjects (military training included); and (d) at least 27 semester hours of elective courses. 

Option B. The recreational program includes courses totaling (a) 

30 semester hours of psychology, education, and sociology; (b) 45% semester hours of physical education; (c) 48 semester hours in the regular sciences and allied subjects (military training included); and (d) at least 21 semester hours of elective courses. 

The completion of any eight-semester course included in the abovedescribed plan, with the proper choice of electives, qualifies the student for a regular high-school teacher's license, first grade, in physical education and one or more other subject groups, as authorized by the Indiana 

State Board of Education. 

In cooperation with the School of Science, a combined plan of study is offered* whereby a student may qualify for the degree of Bachelor of Science and, at the same time, meet the requirements for regular high-school licenses in physical education and in one or more other subject groups. (See the announcement for the School of Science, page 333.) 

*The Department of Physical Education for Women offers to women students in the Schools of Science and Home Economics who are fulfilling the requirements for a state teacher's license in a selected group, elective courses which meet the license requirements in physical education. For details see options listed under the School of Science and the School of Home 

Economics.

TRADE AND INDUSTRIAL EDUCATION 

semester hours)

The Division of Education and Applied Psychology is responsible for the administration of the curriculum in Trade and Industrial Education. This curriculum is intended primarily for prospective teachers in the public schools and for training-personnel in industry. 

Purdue University has been designated by the Indiana State Board for Vocational Education as a training center for vocational trade and industrial education teachers in full conformity with approved State and Federal plans prescribed within the State and Federal vocational education laws. Purdue University receives aid from vocational education funds provided under Smith-Hughes and other Federal laws. The four-year curriculum in Trade and Industrial Education fulfills the pro fessional training requirements specified by the Indiana State Teacher Training and Licensing Commission for a teacher's license in the various fields of vocational education. It also entitles the graduate to the degree of Bachelor of Science in Trade and Industrial Education. (For license requirements in Indiana, see State Department of Education Bulletin 192: 

The Requirements for Teacher Training in Indiana.) The first four semesters in the Trade and Industrial Education curriculum are the same for all students, except that the Division of Education and Applied Psychology, which administers the curriculum, reserves the right to modify the curriculum in terms of individual circumstances. Courses required are basic and include English, mathematics, physics, psychology, education, and shop and drawing courses. Before the end of the fourth semester the student decides on his objective, and with the curriculum adviser (Chairman for Trade and Industrial 

Education) plans the last four semesters of the curriculum. If and when the objective of a student changes, within the intent of the curriculum, corresponding changes may be expected in the plans for the remaining semesters.

The last four semesters of the curriculum (the junior and senior years) contain certain courses required of all students, and also provide for a liberal selection of electives. The electives make it possible for the student to better satisfy individual needs. The choice of electives is made with the advice and approval of the Chairman for Trade and Industrial Education, and subject to the approval of the Director of the 

Division of Education and Applied Psychology. 

In addition to the courses offered on the campus, certain designated professional courses are offered through the itinerant teacher training staff on a field service basis. These courses, when taken for credit and satisfactorily completed, may apply toward graduation in Trade and Industrial Education or toward a Master's degree with a major or a minor in Trade and Industrial Education (see Graduate Bulletin). These field service courses are identified as such as they appear in the course descriptions for the Division of Education and Applied Psychology.

NAVAL SCIENCE AND TACTICS NAVAL RESERVE OFFICERS' TRAINING CORPS The Naval Science Department, as part of the Naval Reserve Officers' 

Training Corps, was established at Purdue University on November 1, 1945. Its mission is to provide, by training and instruction in essential naval subjects, a source from which qualified officers may be obtained for the U. S. Navy or Marine Corps or for the Naval Reserve or Marine 

Corps Reserve. 

Subjects and outlines of Naval Science courses are prescribed by the Bureau of Naval Personnel. In general, each course carries a credit of three semester hours, which, up to twenty-four hours, is (1) counted as a credit toward the Degree of Bachelor of Naval Science and Tactics, and (2) with the approval of the deans concerned may be used as electives or as substitutes for required courses leading to the Bachelor of Science degrees in the several schools of the University. 

For further details see page 248. 351

DIVISION OF TECHNICAL INSTITUTES 

The Division of Technical Institutes offers six curricula leading to the Associate Technical Aide and Technical Aide diplomas. These cur ricula provide post-high-school technological training. They serve persons who wish to prepare themselves in two or three years for activities and responsibilities requiring more preparation than that demanded of skilled craftsmen and less than that needed by graduate engineers. They also provide in-service training for adults. These curricula are designed to prepare persons chiefly for technical, supervisory, or managerial services. 

The Division of Technical Institutes is administered by the Division of Technical Extension, but uses the talent and experience of the engineering and other staffs of the University.

High-school graduation is a prerequisite for admission. Credit earned in Technical Institute classes applies to Technical Institute diplomas. A 

greater emphasis is placed upon practical application of the subject matter and less upon the theoretical aspects than in the engineering programs. Two years of full-time day study are available, although all programs are also offered on a part-time evening basis. In addition a third year of study is available on a part-time evening basis. 

Complete programs are available at extension centers in Fort Wayne, Hammond, Indianapolis, Michigan City, and Muncie. In general, the programs of study offered in any center are determined by the community needs and the local industrial activity. Altogether, six fields of specialization are available: I. Production Planning Technology; II. Drafting and Mechanical Technology; III. Electrical Technology; IV. Industrial Technology; V. Chemical and Metallurgical Technology; VI. Building 

Construction Technology. The plan of study for each of these fields of specialization has two functions: one, to give the student fundamental technical instruction; and, two, to give him intensive training in one specialized field. The fundamental courses are common to all fields, as are certain non-technical courses. In order to provide flexibility, instruction is given in three regular 12-week terms each year. Six terms of work qualify a student for the Associate Technical Aide diploma. A student must select his field of specialization before starting work. 352
